</tr><tr><td class="sidebar-navbar"><link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1129693374"><style data-mw-deduplicate="TemplateStyles:r1063604349">.mw-parser-output .navbar{display:inline;font-size:88%;font-weight:normal}.mw-parser-output .navbar-collapse{float:left;text-align:left}.mw-parser-output .navbar-boxtext{word-spacing:0}.mw-parser-output .navbar ul{display:inline-block;white-space:nowrap;line-height:inherit}.mw-parser-output .navbar-brackets::before{margin-right:-0.125em;content:"[ "}.mw-parser-output .navbar-brackets::after{margin-left:-0.125em;content:" ]"}.mw-parser-output .navbar li{word-spacing:-0.125em}.mw-parser-output .navbar a>span,.mw-parser-output .navbar a>abbr{text-decoration:inherit}.mw-parser-output .navbar-mini abbr{font-variant:small-caps;border-bottom:none;text-decoration:none;cursor:inherit}.mw-parser-output .navbar-ct-full{font-size:114%;margin:0 7em}.mw-parser-output .navbar-ct-mini{font-size:114%;margin:0 4em}</style><div class="navbar plainlinks hlist navbar-mini"><ul><li class="nv-view"><a href="/wiki/Template:Boris_Johnson_sidebar" title="Template:Boris Johnson sidebar"><abbr title="View this template">v</abbr></a></li><li class="nv-talk"><a href="/wiki/Template_talk:Boris_Johnson_sidebar" title="Template talk:Boris Johnson sidebar"><abbr title="Discuss this template">t</abbr></a></li><li class="nv-edit"><a class="external text" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Template:Boris_Johnson_sidebar&amp;action=edit"><abbr title="Edit this template">e</abbr></a></li></ul></div></td></tr></tbody></table>
<p><b>Alexander Boris de Pfeffel Johnson</b>  (<span class="rt-commentedText nowrap"><span class="IPA nopopups noexcerpt" lang="en-fonipa"><a href="/wiki/Help:IPA/English" title="Help:IPA/English">/<span style="border-bottom:1px dotted"><span title="/ˈ/: primary stress follows">ˈ</span><span title="&#39;f&#39; in &#39;find&#39;">f</span><span title="/ɛ/: &#39;e&#39; in &#39;dress&#39;">ɛ</span><span title="&#39;f&#39; in &#39;find&#39;">f</span><span title="/əl/: &#39;le&#39; in &#39;bottle&#39;">əl</span></span>/</a></span></span>,<sup id="cite_ref-Who_Do_You_Think_You_Are?_3-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Who_Do_You_Think_You_Are?-3">&#91;2&#93;</a></sup> born 19 June 1964) is a British politician and writer who served as <a href="/wiki/Prime_Minister_of_the_United_Kingdom" title="Prime Minister of the United Kingdom">Prime Minister of the United Kingdom</a> and <a href="/wiki/Leader_of_the_Conservative_Party_(UK)" title="Leader of the Conservative Party (UK)">Leader of the Conservative Party</a> from 2019 to 2022. He previously served as <a href="/wiki/Foreign_Secretary" title="Foreign Secretary">Foreign Secretary</a> from 2016 to 2018 and as <a href="/wiki/Mayor_of_London" title="Mayor of London">Mayor of London</a> from 2008 to 2016. He was <a href="/wiki/Member_of_Parliament_(United_Kingdom)" title="Member of Parliament (United Kingdom)">Member of Parliament</a> (MP) for <a href="/wiki/Uxbridge_and_South_Ruislip_(UK_Parliament_constituency)" title="Uxbridge and South Ruislip (UK Parliament constituency)">Uxbridge and South Ruislip</a> from 2015 to 2023, having previously been MP for <a href="/wiki/Henley_(UK_Parliament_constituency)" title="Henley (UK Parliament constituency)">Henley</a> from 2001 to 2008.
</p><p>Johnson attended <a href="/wiki/Eton_College" title="Eton College">Eton College</a> and studied <a href="/wiki/Literae_Humaniores" class="mw-redirect" title="Literae Humaniores">Classics</a> at <a href="/wiki/Balliol_College,_Oxford" title="Balliol College, Oxford">Balliol College, Oxford</a>. He was elected <a href="/wiki/List_of_presidents_of_the_Oxford_Union" title="List of presidents of the Oxford Union">president of the Oxford Union</a> in 1986. In 1989, he became the Brussels correspondent – and later political columnist – for <i><a href="/wiki/The_Daily_Telegraph" title="The Daily Telegraph">The Daily Telegraph</a></i>, and from 1999 to 2005 he was the editor of <i><a href="/wiki/The_Spectator" title="The Spectator">The Spectator</a></i>. Following his election to Parliament in 2001, he became a member of the <a href="/wiki/Shadow_cabinet" title="Shadow cabinet">shadow cabinets</a> of <a href="/wiki/Michael_Howard" title="Michael Howard">Michael Howard</a> and later <a href="/wiki/David_Cameron" title="David Cameron">David Cameron</a>. Johnson <a href="/wiki/2008_London_mayoral_election" title="2008 London mayoral election">was elected Mayor of London in 2008</a> and resigned from the House of Commons. He was <a href="/wiki/2012_London_mayoral_election" title="2012 London mayoral election">re-elected mayor in 2012.</a> In the <a href="/wiki/2015_United_Kingdom_general_election" title="2015 United Kingdom general election">2015 general election</a> he was elected MP for Uxbridge and South Ruislip, and the following year did not seek re-election as mayor. Johnson was a prominent figure in the successful <a href="/wiki/Vote_Leave" title="Vote Leave">Vote Leave</a> campaign for <a href="/wiki/Brexit" title="Brexit">Brexit</a> in the <a href="/wiki/2016_United_Kingdom_European_Union_membership_referendum" title="2016 United Kingdom European Union membership referendum">2016 European Union membership referendum</a>. After the referendum, Prime Minister <a href="/wiki/Theresa_May" title="Theresa May">Theresa May</a> appointed him foreign secretary in her <a href="/wiki/First_May_ministry" title="First May ministry">cabinet</a>. He resigned from the position in 2018 in protest at both the <a href="/wiki/Chequers_Agreement" class="mw-redirect" title="Chequers Agreement">Chequers Agreement</a> and May's approach to Brexit.
</p><p>Johnson defeated <a href="/wiki/Jeremy_Hunt" title="Jeremy Hunt">Jeremy Hunt</a> in the <a href="/wiki/2019_Conservative_Party_leadership_election" title="2019 Conservative Party leadership election">2019 Conservative Party leadership election</a> to succeed May, who resigned after Parliament's repeated rejections of her <a href="/wiki/Brexit_withdrawal_agreement" title="Brexit withdrawal agreement">Brexit withdrawal agreement</a>. Johnson <a href="/wiki/Brexit_negotiations_in_2019" title="Brexit negotiations in 2019">re-opened Brexit negotiations</a> and in early September <a href="/wiki/2019_British_prorogation_controversy" title="2019 British prorogation controversy">prorogued Parliament</a>, with the <a href="/wiki/Supreme_Court_of_the_United_Kingdom" title="Supreme Court of the United Kingdom">Supreme Court</a> later that month ruling the action to have been unlawful.<sup id="cite_ref-prorogationtechnicality_5-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-prorogationtechnicality-5">&#91;b&#93;</a></sup> After agreeing to a revised Brexit withdrawal agreement which replaced the <a href="/wiki/Irish_backstop" title="Irish backstop">Irish backstop</a> with the <a href="/wiki/Northern_Ireland_Protocol" title="Northern Ireland Protocol">Northern Ireland Protocol</a>, but <a href="/wiki/Parliamentary_votes_on_Brexit" title="Parliamentary votes on Brexit">failing to win parliamentary support</a> for the agreement, Johnson called a <a href="/wiki/Snap_election" title="Snap election">snap general election</a> to be held in December 2019. In <a href="/wiki/2019_United_Kingdom_general_election" title="2019 United Kingdom general election">the election</a>, he led the Conservative Party to their largest victory since <a href="/wiki/1987_United_Kingdom_general_election" title="1987 United Kingdom general election">1987</a>. On 31 January 2020, the United Kingdom withdrew from the European Union and entered a transition period of <a href="/wiki/Trade_negotiation_between_the_UK_and_the_EU" title="Trade negotiation between the UK and the EU">trade negotiations</a> that led to the <a href="/wiki/EU%E2%80%93UK_Trade_and_Cooperation_Agreement" title="EU–UK Trade and Cooperation Agreement">EU–UK Trade and Cooperation Agreement</a>.
</p><p>A decisive event that occurred during Johnson's premiership was the <a href="/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_Kingdom" title="COVID-19 pandemic in the United Kingdom">COVID-19 pandemic</a>. The government <a href="/wiki/British_government_response_to_the_COVID-19_pandemic" title="British government response to the COVID-19 pandemic">responded</a> to the pandemic by introducing various <a href="/wiki/Coronavirus_Act_2020" title="Coronavirus Act 2020">emergency powers</a> and measures across the country to mitigate its impact and approved the rollout of a <a href="/wiki/COVID-19_vaccination_in_the_United_Kingdom" title="COVID-19 vaccination in the United Kingdom">nationwide vaccination programme</a>. He also responded to the <a href="/wiki/Russian_invasion_of_Ukraine" title="Russian invasion of Ukraine">Russian invasion of Ukraine</a> by imposing <a href="/wiki/International_sanctions_during_the_2022_Russian_invasion_of_Ukraine" class="mw-redirect" title="International sanctions during the 2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine">sanctions on Russia</a> and authorising <a href="/wiki/List_of_foreign_aid_to_Ukraine_during_the_Russo-Ukrainian_War" class="mw-redirect" title="List of foreign aid to Ukraine during the Russo-Ukrainian War">foreign aid and weapons shipments</a> to Ukraine.<sup id="cite_ref-6" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-6">&#91;4&#93;</a></sup> In the <a href="/wiki/Partygate" title="Partygate">Partygate</a> scandal it was found that multiple parties had been held at <a href="/wiki/10_Downing_Street" title="10 Downing Street">10 Downing Street</a> during <a href="/wiki/COVID-19_lockdown_in_the_United_Kingdom" title="COVID-19 lockdown in the United Kingdom">national COVID-19 lockdowns</a>, and COVID-19 social distancing laws were breached by 83 individuals, including Johnson, who in April 2022 was issued with a <a href="/wiki/Fixed_penalty_notice" title="Fixed penalty notice">fixed penalty notice</a>. The publishing of the <a href="/wiki/Sue_Gray_report" class="mw-redirect" title="Sue Gray report">Sue Gray report</a> in May 2022 and a widespread sense of dissatisfaction led in June 2022 to a <a href="/wiki/2022_vote_of_confidence_in_the_Conservative_Party_leadership_of_Boris_Johnson" title="2022 vote of confidence in the Conservative Party leadership of Boris Johnson">vote of confidence</a> in his leadership among Conservative MPs, which he won. In July 2022, revelations over his <a href="/wiki/Chris_Pincher_scandal" title="Chris Pincher scandal">appointment of Chris Pincher</a> as deputy <a href="/wiki/Chief_Whip_of_the_Conservative_Party" title="Chief Whip of the Conservative Party">chief whip</a> while knowing of allegations of sexual misconduct against him led to a <a href="/wiki/July_2022_United_Kingdom_government_crisis" title="July 2022 United Kingdom government crisis">mass resignation of members of the government</a> and to Johnson announcing his resignation as prime minister. He left office on 6 September and was succeeded by Foreign Secretary <a href="/wiki/Liz_Truss" title="Liz Truss">Liz Truss</a>. Johnson remained in the House of Commons as a <a href="/wiki/Backbencher" title="Backbencher">backbencher</a> until he resigned in June 2023, days before the <a href="/wiki/Commons_Privileges_Committee_investigation_into_Boris_Johnson" title="Commons Privileges Committee investigation into Boris Johnson">Privileges Committee investigation</a> unanimously found that he had lied to the <a href="/wiki/House_of_Commons_of_the_United_Kingdom" title="House of Commons of the United Kingdom">House of Commons</a> on numerous occasions.
</p><p>Johnson is a <a href="/wiki/Public_image_of_Boris_Johnson" title="Public image of Boris Johnson">controversial figure</a> in British politics.<sup id="cite_ref-ABC_7-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-ABC-7">&#91;5&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FT_8-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FT-8">&#91;6&#93;</a></sup> His supporters have praised him for being humorous, witty, and entertaining,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEGimson201220_9-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGimson201220-9">&#91;7&#93;</a></sup> with an appeal reaching beyond traditional Conservative Party voters, making him an electoral asset to the party.<sup id="cite_ref-10" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-10">&#91;8&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011327_11-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011327-11">&#91;9&#93;</a></sup> Conversely, his critics have accused him of lying, <a href="/wiki/Elitism" title="Elitism">elitism</a>, <a href="/wiki/Cronyism" title="Cronyism">cronyism</a> and <a href="/wiki/Bigotry" class="mw-redirect" title="Bigotry">bigotry</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEEdwardsIsaby2008110_12-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdwardsIsaby2008110-12">&#91;10&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-GuardChums_13-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-GuardChums-13">&#91;11&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011365_14-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011365-14">&#91;12&#93;</a></sup> As prime minister, his supporters praised him for "<a href="/wiki/Get_Brexit_Done" title="Get Brexit Done">getting Brexit done</a>", overseeing the UK's COVID-19 vaccination programme, which was initially amongst the fastest in the world, and providing global leadership following the Russian invasion of Ukraine.<sup id="cite_ref-15" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-15">&#91;13&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-16" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-16">&#91;14&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-17" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-17">&#91;15&#93;</a></sup> His tenure saw several controversies and scandals, and is viewed as the most scandalous premiership of modern times by historians and biographers.<sup id="cite_ref-Observer-historians2_18-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Observer-historians2-18">&#91;16&#93;</a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Political_positions_of_Boris_Johnson" title="Political positions of Boris Johnson">Johnson's political positions</a> have been described as <a href="/wiki/One-nation_conservative" class="mw-redirect" title="One-nation conservative">one-nation conservative</a>, and commentators have characterised his political style as opportunistic, <a href="/wiki/Populist" class="mw-redirect" title="Populist">populist</a> and pragmatic.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011121_19-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011121-19">&#91;17&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-IT190623_20-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-IT190623-20">&#91;18&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-21" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-21">&#91;19&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<style data-mw-deduplicate="TemplateStyles:r886046785">.mw-parser-output .toclimit-2 .toclevel-1 ul,.mw-parser-output .toclimit-3 .toclevel-2 ul,.mw-parser-output .toclimit-4 .toclevel-3 ul,.mw-parser-output .toclimit-5 .toclevel-4 ul,.mw-parser-output .toclimit-6 .toclevel-5 ul,.mw-parser-output .toclimit-7 .toclevel-6 ul{display:none}</style><div class="toclimit-3"><meta property="mw:PageProp/toc" /></div>
<h2><span class="mw-headline" id="Early_life">Early life</span></h2>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Childhood">Childhood</span></h3>
<p>Alexander Boris de Pfeffel Johnson was born on 19 June 1964 in the <a href="/wiki/Upper_East_Side" title="Upper East Side">Upper East Side</a> of <a href="/wiki/Manhattan" title="Manhattan">Manhattan</a>, New York City,<sup id="cite_ref-22" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-22">&#91;20&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell201110Gimson20121_23-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell201110Gimson20121-23">&#91;21&#93;</a></sup> to 23-year-old <a href="/wiki/Stanley_Johnson_(writer)" title="Stanley Johnson (writer)">Stanley Johnson</a>, then studying economics at <a href="/wiki/Columbia_University" title="Columbia University">Columbia University</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell201111Gimson20122_24-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell201111Gimson20122-24">&#91;22&#93;</a></sup> and 22-year-old <a href="/wiki/Charlotte_Johnson_Wahl" title="Charlotte Johnson Wahl">Charlotte Fawcett</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-telegraph.co.uk_25-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-telegraph.co.uk-25">&#91;23&#93;</a></sup> an artist from a family of liberal intellectuals. Johnson's parents had married in 1963 before moving to the United States.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell201111,_24–25Gimson201212–13_26-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell201111,_24–25Gimson201212–13-26">&#91;24&#93;</a></sup> They returned to the UK in September 1964, so that Charlotte could study at the <a href="/wiki/University_of_Oxford" title="University of Oxford">University of Oxford</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEEdwardsIsaby200844Purnell201112–13Gimson201211_27-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdwardsIsaby200844Purnell201112–13Gimson201211-27">&#91;25&#93;</a></sup> During this time she lived with her son in <a href="/wiki/Summertown,_Oxford" title="Summertown, Oxford">Summertown</a>, a suburb of <a href="/wiki/Oxford" title="Oxford">Oxford</a>, and in September 1965 she gave birth to a daughter, <a href="/wiki/Rachel_Johnson" title="Rachel Johnson">Rachel</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell201113_28-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell201113-28">&#91;26&#93;</a></sup> In July 1965, the family moved to <a href="/wiki/Crouch_End" title="Crouch End">Crouch End</a> in <a href="/wiki/North_London" title="North London">North London</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell201114_29-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell201114-29">&#91;27&#93;</a></sup> and in February 1966 they relocated to Washington, DC, where Stanley had gained employment with the <a href="/wiki/World_Bank" title="World Bank">World Bank</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEEdwardsIsaby200844Purnell201116Gimson201214_30-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdwardsIsaby200844Purnell201116Gimson201214-30">&#91;28&#93;</a></sup> Stanley then took a job with a policy panel on <a href="/wiki/Population_control" title="Population control">population control</a>, and moved the family to <a href="/wiki/Norwalk,_Connecticut" title="Norwalk, Connecticut">Norwalk, Connecticut</a>, in June.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell201116_31-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell201116-31">&#91;29&#93;</a></sup> A third child, Leo, was born in September 1967.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell201115Gimson201214_32-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell201115Gimson201214-32">&#91;30&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-left" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Ashdown_House_-_geograph.org.uk_-_1691918.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2d/Ashdown_House_-_geograph.org.uk_-_1691918.jpg/220px-Ashdown_House_-_geograph.org.uk_-_1691918.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="139" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2d/Ashdown_House_-_geograph.org.uk_-_1691918.jpg/330px-Ashdown_House_-_geograph.org.uk_-_1691918.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2d/Ashdown_House_-_geograph.org.uk_-_1691918.jpg/440px-Ashdown_House_-_geograph.org.uk_-_1691918.jpg 2x" data-file-width="640" data-file-height="404" /></a><figcaption><a href="/wiki/Ashdown_House,_East_Sussex" title="Ashdown House, East Sussex">Ashdown House</a> preparatory school, East Sussex, attended by Johnson from 1975 to 1977</figcaption></figure>
<p>The family returned to the UK in 1969, and they settled into West Nethercote Farm, Somerset, Stanley's remote family home in <a href="/wiki/Exmoor" title="Exmoor">Exmoor</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEEdwardsIsaby200844Purnell201117Gimson201217,_20–22_33-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdwardsIsaby200844Purnell201117Gimson201217,_20–22-33">&#91;31&#93;</a></sup> There, Johnson gained his first experiences of <a href="/wiki/Fox_hunting" title="Fox hunting">fox hunting</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell201118_34-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell201118-34">&#91;32&#93;</a></sup> His father was regularly absent from Nethercote, leaving Johnson to be raised largely by his mother, assisted by <a href="/wiki/Au_pair" title="Au pair">au pairs</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell201118Gimson201225_35-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell201118Gimson201225-35">&#91;33&#93;</a></sup> As a child, Johnson was quiet, studious,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell201114_29-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell201114-29">&#91;27&#93;</a></sup> and deaf, resulting in several operations to insert <a href="/wiki/Tympanostomy_tube" title="Tympanostomy tube">grommets</a> into his ears.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell201113Gimson201211_36-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell201113Gimson201211-36">&#91;34&#93;</a></sup> He and his siblings were encouraged to engage in intellectual activities from a young age,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell201126Gimson201218_37-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell201126Gimson201218-37">&#91;35&#93;</a></sup> with high achievement being greatly valued; Johnson's earliest recorded ambition was to be "world king".<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEEdwardsIsaby200845Purnell201128Gimson201217–18_38-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdwardsIsaby200845Purnell201128Gimson201217–18-38">&#91;36&#93;</a></sup> Having no friends other than their siblings, the children became very close.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell201128–29_39-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell201128–29-39">&#91;37&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In late 1969, the family moved to <a href="/wiki/Maida_Vale" title="Maida Vale">Maida Vale</a> in West London, while Stanley began <a href="/wiki/Postgraduate_education" title="Postgraduate education">post-graduate</a> research at the <a href="/wiki/London_School_of_Economics" title="London School of Economics">London School of Economics</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell201129_40-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell201129-40">&#91;38&#93;</a></sup> In 1970, Charlotte and the children briefly returned to Nethercote, where Johnson attended Winsford Village School, before returning to London to settle in <a href="/wiki/Primrose_Hill" title="Primrose Hill">Primrose Hill</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell201130_41-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell201130-41">&#91;39&#93;</a></sup> where they were educated at Primrose Hill Primary School.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEEdwardsIsaby200844Purnell201130Gimson201226_42-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdwardsIsaby200844Purnell201130Gimson201226-42">&#91;40&#93;</a></sup> A fourth child and third son, <a href="/wiki/Jo_Johnson" title="Jo Johnson">Joseph</a>, was born in late 1971.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell201131_43-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell201131-43">&#91;41&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>After Stanley secured employment at the <a href="/wiki/European_Commission" title="European Commission">European Commission</a> in April 1973, he moved his family to <a href="/wiki/Uccle" title="Uccle">Uccle</a>, Brussels, where Johnson attended the <a href="/wiki/European_School,_Brussels_I" title="European School, Brussels I">European School, Brussels&#160;I</a> and learnt to speak French.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEEdwardsIsaby200844Purnell201131–32Gimson201226_44-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdwardsIsaby200844Purnell201131–32Gimson201226-44">&#91;42&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-45" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-45">&#91;43&#93;</a></sup> During this time, Charlotte had a <a href="/wiki/Nervous_breakdown" class="mw-redirect" title="Nervous breakdown">nervous breakdown</a> and was hospitalised with <a href="/wiki/Major_depressive_disorder" title="Major depressive disorder">clinical depression</a>, after which Johnson and his siblings were sent back to the UK in 1975 to attend <a href="/wiki/Ashdown_House,_East_Sussex" title="Ashdown House, East Sussex">Ashdown House</a>, a preparatory boarding school in East Sussex.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEEdwardsIsaby200844Purnell201133–35Gimson201227–29_46-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdwardsIsaby200844Purnell201133–35Gimson201227–29-46">&#91;44&#93;</a></sup> There, he developed interests in <a href="/wiki/Rugby_football" title="Rugby football">rugby</a>, <a href="/wiki/Ancient_Greek" title="Ancient Greek">Ancient Greek</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Latin" title="Latin">Latin</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell201142Gimson201230–31_47-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell201142Gimson201230–31-47">&#91;45&#93;</a></sup> While there, the teachers' use of <a href="/wiki/School_corporal_punishment" title="School corporal punishment">corporal punishment</a> appalled him.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell201141Gimson201233_48-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell201141Gimson201233-48">&#91;46&#93;</a></sup> Meanwhile, in December 1978 his parents' relationship broke down; they divorced in 1980,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell201136,_42_49-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell201136,_42-49">&#91;47&#93;</a></sup> and Charlotte moved into a flat in <a href="/wiki/Notting_Hill" title="Notting Hill">Notting Hill</a>, West London, where her children joined her for much of their time.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEEdwardsIsaby200844–45Purnell201138–39Gimson201235_50-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdwardsIsaby200844–45Purnell201138–39Gimson201235-50">&#91;48&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span id="Eton_and_Oxford:_1977.E2.80.931987"></span><span class="mw-headline" id="Eton_and_Oxford:_1977–1987">Eton and Oxford: 1977–1987</span></h3>
<style data-mw-deduplicate="TemplateStyles:r1062260506">.mw-parser-output .quotebox{background-color:#F9F9F9;border:1px solid #aaa;box-sizing:border-box;padding:10px;font-size:88%;max-width:100%}.mw-parser-output .quotebox.floatleft{margin:.5em 1.4em .8em 0}.mw-parser-output .quotebox.floatright{margin:.5em 0 .8em 1.4em}.mw-parser-output .quotebox.centered{overflow:hidden;position:relative;margin:.5em auto .8em auto}.mw-parser-output .quotebox.floatleft span,.mw-parser-output .quotebox.floatright span{font-style:inherit}.mw-parser-output .quotebox>blockquote{margin:0;padding:0;border-left:0;font-family:inherit;font-size:inherit}.mw-parser-output .quotebox-title{background-color:#F9F9F9;text-align:center;font-size:110%;font-weight:bold}.mw-parser-output .quotebox-quote>:first-child{margin-top:0}.mw-parser-output .quotebox-quote:last-child>:last-child{margin-bottom:0}.mw-parser-output .quotebox-quote.quoted:before{font-family:"Times New Roman",serif;font-weight:bold;font-size:large;color:gray;content:" “ ";vertical-align:-45%;line-height:0}.mw-parser-output .quotebox-quote.quoted:after{font-family:"Times New Roman",serif;font-weight:bold;font-size:large;color:gray;content:" ” ";line-height:0}.mw-parser-output .quotebox .left-aligned{text-align:left}.mw-parser-output .quotebox .right-aligned{text-align:right}.mw-parser-output .quotebox .center-aligned{text-align:center}.mw-parser-output .quotebox .quote-title,.mw-parser-output .quotebox .quotebox-quote{display:block}.mw-parser-output .quotebox cite{display:block;font-style:normal}@media screen and (max-width:640px){.mw-parser-output .quotebox{width:100%!important;margin:0 0 .8em!important;float:none!important}}</style><div class="quotebox pullquote floatright" style="width:25em; ;">
<blockquote class="quotebox-quote left-aligned" style="">
<p>As a kid I was extremely spotty, extremely nerdy and horribly <a href="https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/swotty#English" class="extiw" title="wikt:swotty">swotty</a>. My idea of a really good time was to travel across London on the tube to visit the <a href="/wiki/British_Museum" title="British Museum">British Museum</a>.
</p>
</blockquote>
<p><cite class="left-aligned" style="">—&#8201;Boris Johnson<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell201149_51-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell201149-51">&#91;49&#93;</a></sup></cite>
</p>
</div>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-right" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Oxford_-_Balliol_College_-_geograph.org.uk_-_1329613.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7f/Oxford_-_Balliol_College_-_geograph.org.uk_-_1329613.jpg/220px-Oxford_-_Balliol_College_-_geograph.org.uk_-_1329613.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="147" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7f/Oxford_-_Balliol_College_-_geograph.org.uk_-_1329613.jpg/330px-Oxford_-_Balliol_College_-_geograph.org.uk_-_1329613.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7f/Oxford_-_Balliol_College_-_geograph.org.uk_-_1329613.jpg/440px-Oxford_-_Balliol_College_-_geograph.org.uk_-_1329613.jpg 2x" data-file-width="640" data-file-height="427" /></a><figcaption>Johnson read Classics at <a href="/wiki/Balliol_College,_Oxford" title="Balliol College, Oxford">Balliol College, Oxford</a>.</figcaption></figure>
<p>Johnson gained a <a href="/wiki/King%27s_Scholar" title="King&#39;s Scholar">King's Scholarship</a> to study at <a href="/wiki/Eton_College" title="Eton College">Eton College</a>, a boarding school near <a href="/wiki/Windsor,_Berkshire" title="Windsor, Berkshire">Windsor</a> in Berkshire.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEEdwardsIsaby200844Purnell201142_52-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdwardsIsaby200844Purnell201142-52">&#91;50&#93;</a></sup> Arriving in the autumn term of 1977,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell201145_53-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell201145-53">&#91;51&#93;</a></sup> he began using his middle name Boris rather than his first name Alexander,<sup id="cite_ref-54" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-54">&#91;52&#93;</a></sup> and developed "the eccentric English persona" for which he became famous.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell201147–48_55-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell201147–48-55">&#91;53&#93;</a></sup> He denounced his Catholic faith and became an <a href="/wiki/Anglicanism" title="Anglicanism">Anglican</a>, joining the <a href="/wiki/Church_of_England" title="Church of England">Church of England</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell201148_56-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell201148-56">&#91;54&#93;</a></sup> School reports complained about his idleness, complacency, and lateness,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEEdwardsIsaby200844Purnell201150–51Gimson201241–44_57-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdwardsIsaby200844Purnell201150–51Gimson201241–44-57">&#91;55&#93;</a></sup> but he was popular and well known at Eton.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell201147–48_55-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell201147–48-55">&#91;53&#93;</a></sup> 
</p><p>Johnson's friends were largely from the wealthy upper classes; his best friends being <a href="/wiki/Darius_Guppy" title="Darius Guppy">Darius Guppy</a> and <a href="/wiki/Charles_Spencer,_9th_Earl_Spencer" title="Charles Spencer, 9th Earl Spencer">Charles Spencer</a>, both of whom later accompanied him at the <a href="/wiki/University_of_Oxford" title="University of Oxford">University of Oxford</a> and remained friends into adulthood.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell201153_58-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell201153-58">&#91;56&#93;</a></sup> Johnson excelled in <a href="/wiki/English_studies" title="English studies">English</a> and the <a href="/wiki/Classics" title="Classics">Classics</a>, winning prizes in both,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell201149–50_59-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell201149–50-59">&#91;57&#93;</a></sup> and became secretary of the school <a href="/wiki/Debating_society" class="mw-redirect" title="Debating society">debating society</a><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell201155_60-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell201155-60">&#91;58&#93;</a></sup> and editor of the school newspaper, <i>The Eton College Chronicle</i>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell201149,_53_61-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell201149,_53-61">&#91;59&#93;</a></sup> In late 1981, he became a member of <a href="/wiki/Eton_Society" class="mw-redirect" title="Eton Society"><i>Pop</i></a>,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell201154–55Gimson201251–52_62-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell201154–55Gimson201251–52-62">&#91;60&#93;</a></sup> a small, self-selecting elite and glamorous group of prefects. Later in Johnson's career it was a point of rivalry with <a href="/wiki/David_Cameron" title="David Cameron">David Cameron</a>, who had failed to enter <i>Pop</i>. After leaving Eton, Johnson went on a <a href="/wiki/Gap_year" title="Gap year">gap year</a> to Australia, where he taught English and Latin at <a href="/wiki/Timbertop_(Geelong_Grammar_School)" class="mw-redirect" title="Timbertop (Geelong Grammar School)">Timbertop</a>, an <a href="/wiki/Outward_Bound" title="Outward Bound">Outward Bound</a>-inspired campus of <a href="/wiki/Geelong_Grammar_School" title="Geelong Grammar School">Geelong Grammar</a>, an independent boarding school.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell201158–59_63-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell201158–59-63">&#91;61&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-64" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-64">&#91;62&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-65" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-65">&#91;63&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Johnson won a scholarship to study <i><a href="/wiki/Literae_Humaniores" class="mw-redirect" title="Literae Humaniores">Literae Humaniores</a></i> at <a href="/wiki/Balliol_College,_Oxford" title="Balliol College, Oxford">Balliol College, Oxford</a>, a four-year course in the study of the Classics, ancient languages, literature, history, and philosophy.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEEdwardsIsaby200845Purnell201157Gimson201283_66-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdwardsIsaby200845Purnell201157Gimson201283-66">&#91;64&#93;</a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Matriculating" class="mw-redirect" title="Matriculating">Matriculating</a> at the university in late 1983,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEGimson201256_67-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGimson201256-67">&#91;65&#93;</a></sup> he was one of a generation of Oxford undergraduates who were later to dominate British politics and media in the second decade of the 21st century; among them David Cameron, <a href="/wiki/William_Hague" title="William Hague">William Hague</a>, <a href="/wiki/Michael_Gove" title="Michael Gove">Michael Gove</a>, <a href="/wiki/Jeremy_Hunt" title="Jeremy Hunt">Jeremy Hunt</a> and <a href="/wiki/Nick_Boles" title="Nick Boles">Nick Boles</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell201162_68-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell201162-68">&#91;66&#93;</a></sup> While at Oxford, Johnson participated in college <a href="/wiki/Rugby_union" title="Rugby union">rugby union</a>, playing as a <a href="/wiki/Prop_(rugby_union)" class="mw-redirect" title="Prop (rugby union)">tighthead prop</a> for <a href="/wiki/Balliol_College,_Oxford" title="Balliol College, Oxford">Balliol College</a>'s team for four years.<sup id="cite_ref-69" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-69">&#91;67&#93;</a></sup> To his later regret, he joined <a href="/wiki/Bullingdon_Club" title="Bullingdon Club">Bullingdon Club</a>, an exclusive drinking society notorious for acts of vandalism on host premises.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell201163–65Gimson201263–66_70-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell201163–65Gimson201263–66-70">&#91;68&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-71" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-71">&#91;69&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-72" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-72">&#91;70&#93;</a></sup> Many years later, <a href="/wiki/1987_Bullingdon_Club_photograph" title="1987 Bullingdon Club photograph">a group photograph</a> including himself and Cameron in Bullingdon Club formal dress led to much negative coverage from the press. He began a relationship with <a href="/wiki/Allegra_Mostyn-Owen" title="Allegra Mostyn-Owen">Allegra Mostyn-Owen</a>, cover girl for <i><a href="/wiki/Tatler" title="Tatler">Tatler</a></i> magazine and daughter of <a href="/wiki/Christie%27s_Education" class="mw-redirect" title="Christie&#39;s Education">Christie's Education</a> chairman <a href="/wiki/William_Mostyn-Owen" title="William Mostyn-Owen">William Mostyn-Owen</a>. She was a glamorous and popular student from his own social background, and they became engaged while at university.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell201172,_74–78Gimson201276–83_73-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell201172,_74–78Gimson201276–83-73">&#91;71&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Johnson was popular and well known at Oxford.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell201170Gimson201260_74-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell201170Gimson201260-74">&#91;72&#93;</a></sup> Alongside Guppy, he edited the university's satirical magazine <i>Tributary</i>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell201168Gimson201274_75-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell201168Gimson201274-75">&#91;73&#93;</a></sup> In 1984, Johnson was elected secretary of the <a href="/wiki/Oxford_Union" title="Oxford Union">Oxford Union</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell201170–71_76-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell201170–71-76">&#91;74&#93;</a></sup> and campaigned unsuccessfully for the career-enhancing and important position of <a href="/wiki/List_of_Presidents_of_the_Oxford_Union" class="mw-redirect" title="List of Presidents of the Oxford Union">Union President</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell201171–73_77-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell201171–73-77">&#91;75&#93;</a></sup> In 1986, Johnson ran successfully for President,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell201180–81_78-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell201180–81-78">&#91;76&#93;</a></sup> but his term was not distinguished or memorable,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell201184_79-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell201184-79">&#91;77&#93;</a></sup> and questions were raised regarding his competence and seriousness.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell201187_80-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell201187-80">&#91;78&#93;</a></sup> At graduation, Johnson was awarded an <a href="/wiki/Upper_second-class_honours" class="mw-redirect" title="Upper second-class honours">upper second-class</a> degree,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell201189–90Gimson201284_81-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell201189–90Gimson201284-81">&#91;79&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-82" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-82">&#91;80&#93;</a></sup> and was deeply unhappy he did not receive a first.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell201192_83-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell201192-83">&#91;81&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h2><span class="mw-headline" id="Early_career">Early career</span></h2>
<h3><span id="The_Times_and_The_Daily_Telegraph:_1987.E2.80.931994"></span><span class="mw-headline" id="The_Times_and_The_Daily_Telegraph:_1987–1994"><i>The Times</i> and <i>The Daily Telegraph</i>: 1987–1994</span></h3>
<p>In September 1987, Johnson and Mostyn-Owen were married in <a href="/wiki/West_Felton" title="West Felton">West Felton</a>, Shropshire, accompanied by a duet for violin and viola <i>Allegra e Boris</i><sup id="cite_ref-84" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-84">&#91;82&#93;</a></sup> specially commissioned for the wedding from <a href="/wiki/Hans_Werner_Henze" title="Hans Werner Henze">Hans Werner Henze</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell201192–94Gimson201285–86_85-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell201192–94Gimson201285–86-85">&#91;83&#93;</a></sup> After a honeymoon in Egypt, they settled in <a href="/wiki/West_Kensington" title="West Kensington">West Kensington</a>, London,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell201194_86-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell201194-86">&#91;84&#93;</a></sup> where he secured work for a <a href="/wiki/Management_consultancy" class="mw-redirect" title="Management consultancy">management consultancy</a> company, <a href="/wiki/L.E.K._Consulting" title="L.E.K. Consulting">L.E.K. Consulting</a>; he resigned after a week.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEEdwardsIsaby200846Purnell201194–95Gimson201287–88_87-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdwardsIsaby200846Purnell201194–95Gimson201287–88-87">&#91;85&#93;</a></sup> In late 1987, through family connections, he began work as a graduate trainee at <i><a href="/wiki/The_Times" title="The Times">The Times</a></i>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell201195–99Gimson201288–90_88-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell201195–99Gimson201288–90-88">&#91;86&#93;</a></sup> Scandal erupted when Johnson wrote an article for the newspaper, on the <a href="/wiki/Archaeological" class="mw-redirect" title="Archaeological">archaeological</a> discovery of <a href="/wiki/Edward_II_of_England" title="Edward II of England">Edward II</a>'s palace, having invented a quote for the article which he falsely attributed to the historian <a href="/wiki/Colin_Lucas" title="Colin Lucas">Colin Lucas</a>, his godfather. After the editor <a href="/wiki/Charles_Wilson_(journalist)" title="Charles Wilson (journalist)">Charles Wilson</a> learnt of the matter, he dismissed Johnson.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011100–102Gimson201290–96_89-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011100–102Gimson201290–96-89">&#91;87&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Johnson secured employment on the leader-writing desk of <i><a href="/wiki/The_Daily_Telegraph" title="The Daily Telegraph">The Daily Telegraph</a></i>, having met its editor, <a href="/wiki/Max_Hastings" title="Max Hastings">Max Hastings</a>, while at Oxford University.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011102–103Gimson201297_90-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011102–103Gimson201297-90">&#91;88&#93;</a></sup> His articles appealed to the newspaper's conservative, middle-class, middle-aged "<a href="/wiki/Middle_England" title="Middle England">Middle England</a>" readership,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011108_91-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011108-91">&#91;89&#93;</a></sup> and were known for their distinctive literary style, replete with old-fashioned words and phrases and for regularly referring to the readership as "my friends".<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011106–107_92-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011106–107-92">&#91;90&#93;</a></sup> In early 1989, Johnson was appointed to the newspaper's Brussels bureau to report on the European Commission,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011109_93-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011109-93">&#91;91&#93;</a></sup> remaining in the post until 1994.<sup id="cite_ref-Fletcher_94-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Fletcher-94">&#91;92&#93;</a></sup> A strong critic of the integrationist Commission president <a href="/wiki/Jacques_Delors" title="Jacques Delors">Jacques Delors</a>, he established himself as one of the city's few <a href="/wiki/Eurosceptic" class="mw-redirect" title="Eurosceptic">Eurosceptic</a> journalists.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011115–116_95-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011115–116-95">&#91;93&#93;</a></sup> He wrote articles about <a href="/wiki/Euromyths" class="mw-redirect" title="Euromyths">euromyths</a> such as the EU wanting to ban <a href="/wiki/Prawn_cocktail" title="Prawn cocktail">prawn cocktail</a> crisps and British sausages, and to standardise condom sizes because Italians had smaller penises.<sup id="cite_ref-96" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-96">&#91;94&#93;</a></sup> He wrote that Brussels had recruited sniffers to ensure that Euro-manure smells the same,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBower202168,_627_97-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBower202168,_627-97">&#91;95&#93;</a></sup> and that the Eurocrats were about to dictate the acceptable curve of bananas<sup id="cite_ref-99" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-99">&#91;c&#93;</a></sup> and the limits on the power of vacuum cleaners,<sup id="cite_ref-100" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-100">&#91;97&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-103" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-103">&#91;d&#93;</a></sup> and to order women to return their old sex toys.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBower202168,_627_97-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBower202168,_627-97">&#91;95&#93;</a></sup> He wrote that euro notes made people impotent, that euro coins made people sick, and that a plan to blow up the <a href="/wiki/Berlaymont_building" title="Berlaymont building">Berlaymont building</a> was in place because asbestos cladding made the building too dangerous to inhabit.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBower202168,_627_97-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBower202168,_627-97">&#91;95&#93;</a></sup> Many of his fellow journalists there were critical of his articles, opining they often contained lies designed to discredit the commission.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011121,_126Gimson201298–99,_100–101_104-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011121,_126Gimson201298–99,_100–101-104">&#91;100&#93;</a></sup> The Europhile Conservative politician <a href="/wiki/Chris_Patten" title="Chris Patten">Chris Patten</a> later stated at that time Johnson was "one of the greatest exponents of fake journalism".<sup id="cite_ref-Fletcher_94-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Fletcher-94">&#91;92&#93;</a></sup> Johnson opposed banning handguns after the <a href="/wiki/Dunblane_school_massacre" class="mw-redirect" title="Dunblane school massacre">Dunblane school massacre</a>, writing in his column "Nanny is confiscating their toys. It is like one of those vast <a href="/wiki/Compulsory_sterilization#India" title="Compulsory sterilization">Indian programmes of compulsory vasectomy</a>."<sup id="cite_ref-105" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-105">&#91;101&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Johnson's biographer, <a href="/wiki/Andrew_Gimson" title="Andrew Gimson">Andrew Gimson</a>, believed these articles made him "one of [Euroscepticism's] most famous exponents".<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEGimson2012102_106-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGimson2012102-106">&#91;102&#93;</a></sup> According to another one of his biographers, <a href="/wiki/Sonia_Purnell" title="Sonia Purnell">Sonia Purnell</a>, – who was Johnson's Brussels deputy<sup id="cite_ref-Fletcher_94-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Fletcher-94">&#91;92&#93;</a></sup> – he helped make Euroscepticism "an attractive and emotionally resonant cause for the Right", whereas it had been associated previously with the Left.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011115_107-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011115-107">&#91;103&#93;</a></sup> Johnson's articles established him as the favourite journalist of Conservative Prime Minister <a href="/wiki/Margaret_Thatcher" title="Margaret Thatcher">Margaret Thatcher</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011120Gimson2012104_108-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011120Gimson2012104-108">&#91;104&#93;</a></sup> but Johnson annoyed her successor, the Europhile <a href="/wiki/John_Major" title="John Major">John Major</a>, who spent a great deal of time attempting to refute what Johnson said.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011118,_124_109-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011118,_124-109">&#91;105&#93;</a></sup> Johnson's articles exacerbated tensions between the Conservative Party's Eurosceptic and Europhile factions. As a result, he earned the mistrust of many party members.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011124_110-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011124-110">&#91;106&#93;</a></sup> His writings were also a key influence on the emergence of the eurosceptic <a href="/wiki/UK_Independence_Party" title="UK Independence Party">UK Independence Party</a> (UKIP) in the early 1990s.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011115_107-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011115-107">&#91;103&#93;</a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Conrad_Black" title="Conrad Black">Conrad Black</a>, then proprietor of <i>The Daily Telegraph</i>, said Johnson "was such an effective correspondent for us in Brussels that he greatly influenced British opinion on this country's relations with Europe".<sup id="cite_ref-111" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-111">&#91;107&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In February 1990, Johnson's wife Allegra left him; after several attempts at reconciliation, their marriage ended in April 1993.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011129–130,_134Gimson2012107–111,_113–114_112-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011129–130,_134Gimson2012107–111,_113–114-112">&#91;108&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-guardian200218_113-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-guardian200218-113">&#91;109&#93;</a></sup> He then entered a relationship with childhood friend <a href="/wiki/Marina_Wheeler" title="Marina Wheeler">Marina Wheeler</a>, who had moved to Brussels in 1990.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011130–133Gimson2012111–114_114-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011130–133Gimson2012111–114-114">&#91;110&#93;</a></sup> They were married in May 1993 in Horsham, Sussex.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011134Gimson2012114–115_115-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011134Gimson2012114–115-115">&#91;111&#93;</a></sup> Soon after this Marina gave birth to a daughter.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011135Gimson2012115_116-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011135Gimson2012115-116">&#91;112&#93;</a></sup> Johnson and his new wife settled in <a href="/wiki/Islington" title="Islington">Islington</a>, North London,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011142_117-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011142-117">&#91;113&#93;</a></sup> an area known for its association with the left-liberal <a href="/wiki/Intelligentsia" title="Intelligentsia">intelligentsia</a>. Under the influence of this <i>milieu</i> and of his wife, Johnson moved in a more liberal direction on issues such as <a href="/wiki/Climate_change" title="Climate change">climate change</a>, <a href="/wiki/LGBT_rights" class="mw-redirect" title="LGBT rights">LGBT rights</a> and race relations.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011144,_148_118-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011144,_148-118">&#91;114&#93;</a></sup> While in Islington, the couple had three more children, all given the surname Johnson-Wheeler.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011143Gimson2012125_119-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011143Gimson2012125-119">&#91;115&#93;</a></sup> They were sent to the local Canonbury Primary School and then to private secondary schools.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011146–147_120-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011146–147-120">&#91;116&#93;</a></sup> Devoting much time to his children, Johnson wrote a book of verse, <i>The Perils of the Pushy Parents: A Cautionary Tale</i>, which was published to largely poor reviews.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011153_121-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011153-121">&#91;117&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span id="Political_columnist:_1994.E2.80.931999"></span><span class="mw-headline" id="Political_columnist:_1994–1999">Political columnist: 1994–1999</span></h3>
<p>Back in London, Hastings turned down Johnson's request to become a <a href="/wiki/War_reporter" class="mw-redirect" title="War reporter">war reporter</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011139–140_122-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011139–140-122">&#91;118&#93;</a></sup> instead promoting him to the position of assistant editor and chief political columnist.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011161Gimson2012124_123-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011161Gimson2012124-123">&#91;119&#93;</a></sup> Johnson's column received praise for being ideologically eclectic and distinctively written, and earned him a Commentator of the Year Award at the <i><a href="/wiki/What_the_Papers_Say" title="What the Papers Say">What the Papers Say</a></i> awards.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011168Gimson2012125_124-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011168Gimson2012125-124">&#91;120&#93;</a></sup> Some critics condemned his writing style as bigotry; in various columns he used the words "<a href="/wiki/Piccaninnies" class="mw-redirect" title="Piccaninnies">piccaninnies</a>" and "<a href="/wiki/Watermelon_stereotype" title="Watermelon stereotype">watermelon smiles</a>" when referring to Africans, championed European colonialism in Uganda<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011169_125-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011169-125">&#91;121&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-126" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-126">&#91;122&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-127" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-127">&#91;123&#93;</a></sup> and referred to gay men as "tank-topped bumboys".<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011171_128-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011171-128">&#91;124&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Contemplating a political career, in 1993, Johnson outlined his desire to stand as a Conservative candidate to be a <a href="/wiki/Member_of_the_European_Parliament" title="Member of the European Parliament">Member of the European Parliament</a> (MEP) in the <a href="/wiki/1994_European_Parliament_election_in_the_United_Kingdom" title="1994 European Parliament election in the United Kingdom">1994 European Parliament elections</a>. <a href="/wiki/Andrew_Mitchell" title="Andrew Mitchell">Andrew Mitchell</a> convinced Major not to veto Johnson's candidacy, but Johnson could not find a constituency.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011162–165_129-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011162–165-129">&#91;125&#93;</a></sup> He subsequently turned his attention to obtaining a seat in the UK House of Commons. After being rejected as Conservative candidate for <a href="/wiki/Holborn_and_St_Pancras_(UK_Parliament_constituency)" title="Holborn and St Pancras (UK Parliament constituency)">Holborn and St. Pancras</a>, his party selected him the candidate for <a href="/wiki/Clwyd_South_(UK_Parliament_constituency)" title="Clwyd South (UK Parliament constituency)">Clwyd South</a> in north Wales, then a <a href="/wiki/Labour_Party_(UK)" title="Labour Party (UK)">Labour Party</a> <a href="/wiki/Safe_seat" title="Safe seat">safe seat</a>. Spending six weeks campaigning, he attained 9,091 votes (23 per cent) in the <a href="/wiki/1997_United_Kingdom_general_election" title="1997 United Kingdom general election">1997 general election</a>, losing to the Labour candidate.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEEdwardsIsaby200846Purnell2011185–186Gimson2012125_130-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdwardsIsaby200846Purnell2011185–186Gimson2012125-130">&#91;126&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Scandal erupted in June 1995 when a recording of a 1990 telephone conversation between Johnson and his friend <a href="/wiki/Darius_Guppy" title="Darius Guppy">Darius Guppy</a> was made public.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011173–176Gimson2012117–123_131-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011173–176Gimson2012117–123-131">&#91;127&#93;</a></sup> In the conversation, Guppy said that his criminal activities involving insurance fraud were being investigated by <i><a href="/wiki/News_of_the_World" title="News of the World">News of the World</a></i> journalist Stuart Collier, and he asked Johnson to provide him with Collier's private address, seeking to have the latter beaten to the extent of "a couple of black eyes and a cracked rib or something like that". Johnson agreed to supply the information, although he expressed concern that he would be associated with the attack.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011173–176Gimson2012117–123_131-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011173–176Gimson2012117–123-131">&#91;127&#93;</a></sup> When the phone conversation was published in 1995, Johnson stated that ultimately he had not obliged Guppy's request. Hastings reprimanded Johnson but did not dismiss him.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011173–176Gimson2012117–123_131-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011173–176Gimson2012117–123-131">&#91;127&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Johnson was given a regular column in <i><a href="/wiki/The_Spectator" title="The Spectator">The Spectator</a></i>, sister publication to <i>The Daily Telegraph</i>, which attracted mixed reviews and was often thought rushed.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011168_132-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011168-132">&#91;128&#93;</a></sup> In 1999, he was also given a column reviewing new cars in the magazine <i><a href="/wiki/GQ" title="GQ">GQ</a></i>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011171Gimson2012177–178_133-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011171Gimson2012177–178-133">&#91;129&#93;</a></sup> His behaviour regularly disgruntled his editors; the large number of parking fines that Johnson acquired while testing cars frustrated <i>GQ</i> staff.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011171_128-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011171-128">&#91;124&#93;</a></sup> At <i>The Daily Telegraph</i> and <i>The Spectator</i>, he was consistently late delivering his copy, forcing many staff to stay late to accommodate him; some related that if they published without his work included, he would get angry and shout at them with expletives.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011179–181Gimson2012177_134-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011179–181Gimson2012177-134">&#91;130&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Johnson's appearance on an April 1998 episode of the BBC's satirical current affairs show <i><a href="/wiki/Have_I_Got_News_for_You" title="Have I Got News for You">Have I Got News for You</a></i> brought him national fame.<sup id="cite_ref-135" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-135">&#91;131&#93;</a></sup> He was invited back on to later episodes, including as a guest presenter; for his 2003 appearance, Johnson received a nomination for the <a href="/wiki/British_Academy_Television_Award_for_Best_Entertainment_Performance" title="British Academy Television Award for Best Entertainment Performance">BAFTA Television Award for Best Entertainment Performance</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011176–178Gimson2012127–129_136-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011176–178Gimson2012127–129-136">&#91;132&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-137" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-137">&#91;133&#93;</a></sup> After these appearances, he came to be recognised on the street by the public, and was invited to appear on other television shows, such as <i><a href="/wiki/Top_Gear_(2002_TV_series)" title="Top Gear (2002 TV series)">Top Gear</a></i>, <i><a href="/wiki/Parkinson_(TV_series)" title="Parkinson (TV series)">Parkinson</a></i>, <i><a href="/wiki/Breakfast_with_Frost" title="Breakfast with Frost">Breakfast with Frost</a></i>, and the political show <i><a href="/wiki/Question_Time_(TV_programme)" title="Question Time (TV programme)">Question Time</a></i>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011178Gimson2012130_138-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011178Gimson2012130-138">&#91;134&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span id="The_Spectator_and_MP_for_Henley:_1999.E2.80.932008"></span><span class="mw-headline" id="The_Spectator_and_MP_for_Henley:_1999–2008"><i>The Spectator</i> and MP for Henley: 1999–2008</span></h3>
<p>In July 1999, Conrad Black offered Johnson the editorship of <i>The Spectator</i> on the condition he abandon his parliamentary aspirations; Johnson agreed.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011188Gimson2012131_139-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011188Gimson2012131-139">&#91;135&#93;</a></sup> While retaining <i>The Spectator</i><span class="nowrap" style="padding-left:0.1em;">&#39;</span>s traditional right-wing bent, Johnson welcomed contributions from leftist writers and cartoonists.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011198–199_140-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011198–199-140">&#91;136&#93;</a></sup> Under Johnson's editorship, the magazine's circulation grew by 10% to 62,000 and it began to turn a profit.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011191_141-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011191-141">&#91;137&#93;</a></sup> His editorship also drew criticism; some opined that under him <i>The Spectator</i> avoided serious issues,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011204_142-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011204-142">&#91;138&#93;</a></sup> while colleagues became annoyed that he was regularly absent from the office, meetings, and events.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011192,_194_143-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011192,_194-143">&#91;139&#93;</a></sup> He gained a reputation as a poor political pundit because of incorrect political predictions made in the magazine.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011204_142-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011204-142">&#91;138&#93;</a></sup> His father-in-law <a href="/wiki/Charles_Wheeler_(journalist)" title="Charles Wheeler (journalist)">Charles Wheeler</a> and others strongly criticised him for allowing <i>Spectator</i> columnist <a href="/wiki/Taki_Theodoracopulos" title="Taki Theodoracopulos">Taki Theodoracopulos</a> to publish racist and antisemitic language in the magazine.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011193_144-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011193-144">&#91;140&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-145" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-145">&#91;141&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Journalist Charlotte Edwardes wrote in <i>The Times</i> in 2019 alleging that Johnson had squeezed her thigh at a private lunch in the offices of the <i>Spectator</i> in 1999 and that another woman had told her he had done the same to her. A Downing Street spokesman denied the allegation.<sup id="cite_ref-146" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-146">&#91;142&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-147" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-147">&#91;143&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In 2004, Johnson published an editorial in <i>The Spectator</i> after the murder of <a href="/wiki/Ken_Bigley" class="mw-redirect" title="Ken Bigley">Ken Bigley</a> suggesting that Liverpudlians were wallowing in their victim status and also "hooked on grief" over the <a href="/wiki/Hillsborough_disaster" title="Hillsborough disaster">Hillsborough disaster</a>, which Johnson partly blamed on "drunken fans".<sup id="cite_ref-148" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-148">&#91;144&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-149" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-149">&#91;145&#93;</a></sup> In an appendix added to a later edition of his 2005 book about the Roman empire, <i><a href="/wiki/The_Dream_of_Rome" title="The Dream of Rome">The Dream of Rome</a></i>, <a href="/wiki/Tell_MAMA" title="Tell MAMA">Tell MAMA</a> and the <a href="/wiki/Muslim_Council_of_Britain" title="Muslim Council of Britain">Muslim Council of Britain</a> strongly criticised Johnson for arguing <a href="/wiki/Islam" title="Islam">Islam</a> has caused the <a href="/wiki/Muslim_world" title="Muslim world">Muslim world</a> to be "literally centuries behind" the West.<sup id="cite_ref-theguardian_150-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-theguardian-150">&#91;146&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="Becoming_an_MP">Becoming an MP</span></h4>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1062260506"><div class="quotebox pullquote floatright" style="width:25em; ;">
<blockquote class="quotebox-quote left-aligned" style="">
<p>The selection of Boris Johnson&#160;... confirms the Tory Party's increasing weakness for celebrity personalities over the dreary exigencies of politics. Johnson, for all his gifts, is unlikely to grace any future Tory cabinet. Indeed, he is not known for his excessive interest in serious policy matters, and it is hard to see him grubbing away at administrative detail as an obscure, hardworking junior minister for social security. To maintain his funny man reputation he will no doubt find himself refining his <a href="/wiki/Bertie_Wooster" title="Bertie Wooster">Bertie Wooster</a> interpretation to the point where the impersonation becomes the man.
</p>
</blockquote>
<p><cite class="left-aligned" style="">–Max Hastings, <i>London Evening Standard</i>,&#32;<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011219_151-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011219-151">&#91;147&#93;</a></sup></cite>
</p>
</div>
<p>Following <a href="/wiki/Michael_Heseltine" title="Michael Heseltine">Michael Heseltine</a>'s retirement, Johnson decided to stand as Conservative candidate for <a href="/wiki/Henley_(UK_Parliament_constituency)" title="Henley (UK Parliament constituency)">Henley</a>, a Conservative safe seat in <a href="/wiki/Oxfordshire" title="Oxfordshire">Oxfordshire</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011209–210Gimson2012141_152-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011209–210Gimson2012141-152">&#91;148&#93;</a></sup> The local Conservative branch selected him although it was split over Johnson's candidacy. Some thought him amusing and charming while others disliked his flippant attitude and perceived lack of knowledge of the local area.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011211–212_153-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011211–212-153">&#91;149&#93;</a></sup> Assisted by his television fame, Johnson won the seat in the <a href="/wiki/2001_United_Kingdom_general_election" title="2001 United Kingdom general election">2001 general election</a> with a majority of 8,500 votes.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011220–221_154-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011220–221-154">&#91;150&#93;</a></sup> Alongside his Islington home, Johnson bought a farmhouse outside <a href="/wiki/Thame" title="Thame">Thame</a> in his new constituency.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011240_155-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011240-155">&#91;151&#93;</a></sup> He regularly attended Henley social events and occasionally wrote for the <i><a href="/wiki/Henley_Standard" title="Henley Standard">Henley Standard</a></i>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011238_156-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011238-156">&#91;152&#93;</a></sup> His constituency surgeries proved popular, and he joined local campaigns to stop the closure of <a href="/wiki/Royal_Berkshire_NHS_Foundation_Trust" title="Royal Berkshire NHS Foundation Trust">Townlands Hospital</a> and the local <a href="/wiki/Thames_Valley_Air_Ambulance" title="Thames Valley Air Ambulance">air ambulance</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011239_157-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011239-157">&#91;153&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In Parliament, Johnson was appointed to a <a href="/wiki/Standing_committee" class="mw-redirect" title="Standing committee">standing committee</a> assessing the <a href="/wiki/Proceeds_of_Crime_Act_2002" title="Proceeds of Crime Act 2002">Proceeds of Crime Bill</a>, but missed many of its meetings.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011225_158-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011225-158">&#91;154&#93;</a></sup> Despite his credentials as a public speaker, his speeches in the House of Commons were widely deemed lacklustre; Johnson later called them "crap".<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011232–233_159-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011232–233-159">&#91;155&#93;</a></sup> In his first four years as MP, he attended just over half of the Commons votes; in his second term, this declined to 45 per cent.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011230_160-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011230-160">&#91;156&#93;</a></sup> He usually supported the Conservative <a href="/wiki/Party_line_(politics)" title="Party line (politics)">party line</a> but rebelled against it five times in this period.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011231_161-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011231-161">&#91;157&#93;</a></sup> In <a href="/wiki/Free_votes" class="mw-redirect" title="Free votes">free votes</a>, he demonstrated a more socially liberal attitude than many colleagues, supporting the <a href="/wiki/Gender_Recognition_Act_2004" title="Gender Recognition Act 2004">Gender Recognition Act 2004</a> and the repeal of <a href="/wiki/Section_28" title="Section 28">Section 28</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-162" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-162">&#91;158&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-Conservative_Revolts_163-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Conservative_Revolts-163">&#91;159&#93;</a></sup> However, in 2001, Johnson had spoken out against plans to repeal Section 28, saying it was "Labour's appalling agenda, encouraging the teaching of homosexuality in schools".<sup id="cite_ref-164" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-164">&#91;160&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-165" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-165">&#91;161&#93;</a></sup> After initially stating he would not, he <a href="/wiki/British_Parliamentary_approval_for_the_invasion_of_Iraq" class="mw-redirect" title="British Parliamentary approval for the invasion of Iraq">voted in support</a> of the government's plans to join the United States in the <a href="/wiki/2003_invasion_of_Iraq" title="2003 invasion of Iraq">2003 invasion of Iraq</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011240_155-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011240-155">&#91;151&#93;</a></sup> and in April 2003 visited occupied Baghdad.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011149_166-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011149-166">&#91;162&#93;</a></sup> In August 2004, he backed unsuccessful <a href="/wiki/Parliamentary_motion_to_impeach_Tony_Blair" title="Parliamentary motion to impeach Tony Blair">impeachment procedures</a> against Prime Minister <a href="/wiki/Tony_Blair" title="Tony Blair">Tony Blair</a> for "<a href="/wiki/High_crimes_and_misdemeanours" class="mw-redirect" title="High crimes and misdemeanours">high crimes and misdemeanours</a>" regarding the war,<sup id="cite_ref-167" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-167">&#91;163&#93;</a></sup> and in December 2006 described the invasion as "a colossal mistake and misadventure".<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEGimson2012265_168-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGimson2012265-168">&#91;164&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Although labelling Johnson "ineffably duplicitous" for breaking his promise not to become an MP, Black decided not to dismiss him because he "helped promote the magazine and raise its circulation".<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011189,_190_169-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011189,_190-169">&#91;165&#93;</a></sup> Johnson remained editor of <i>The Spectator</i>, also writing columns for <i>The Daily Telegraph</i> and <i>GQ</i>, and making television appearances.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011226_170-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011226-170">&#91;166&#93;</a></sup> His 2001 book, <i><a href="/wiki/Friends,_Voters,_Countrymen" title="Friends, Voters, Countrymen">Friends, Voters, Countrymen: Jottings on the Stump</a></i>, recounted that year's election campaign,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011230Gimson2012145–146_171-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011230Gimson2012145–146-171">&#91;167&#93;</a></sup> while 2003's <i>Lend Me Your Ears</i> collected together previously published columns and articles.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEGimson2012176–177_172-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGimson2012176–177-172">&#91;168&#93;</a></sup> In 2004, <a href="/wiki/HarperCollins" title="HarperCollins">HarperCollins</a> published his first novel: <i><a href="/wiki/Seventy-Two_Virgins" title="Seventy-Two Virgins">Seventy-Two Virgins: A Comedy of Errors</a></i> revolved around the life of a Conservative MP and contained various autobiographical elements.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011249–251Gimson2012189–192_173-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011249–251Gimson2012189–192-173">&#91;169&#93;</a></sup> Responding to critics who argued he was juggling too many jobs, he cited <a href="/wiki/Winston_Churchill" title="Winston Churchill">Winston Churchill</a> and <a href="/wiki/Benjamin_Disraeli" title="Benjamin Disraeli">Benjamin Disraeli</a> as exemplars who combined their political and literary careers.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011227Gimson2012143_174-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011227Gimson2012143-174">&#91;170&#93;</a></sup> To manage the stress, he took up jogging and cycling,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011228_175-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011228-175">&#91;171&#93;</a></sup> and became so well known for the latter that Gimson suggested he was "perhaps the most famous cyclist in Britain".<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEGimson2012182_176-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGimson2012182-176">&#91;172&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Following <a href="/wiki/William_Hague" title="William Hague">William Hague</a>'s resignation as Conservative leader, Johnson backed <a href="/wiki/Kenneth_Clarke" title="Kenneth Clarke">Kenneth Clarke</a>, regarding Clarke as the only candidate capable of winning a general election; the party elected <a href="/wiki/Iain_Duncan_Smith" title="Iain Duncan Smith">Iain Duncan Smith</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011223–224Gimson2012150_177-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011223–224Gimson2012150-177">&#91;173&#93;</a></sup> Johnson had a strained relationship with Duncan Smith, and <i>The Spectator</i> became critical of his party leadership.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011234Gimson2012150_178-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011234Gimson2012150-178">&#91;174&#93;</a></sup> Duncan Smith was removed from his position in November 2003 and was succeeded by <a href="/wiki/Michael_Howard" title="Michael Howard">Michael Howard</a>; Howard deemed Johnson to be the most popular Conservative politician with the electorate and appointed him vice-chairman of the party, responsible for overseeing its electoral campaign.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEEdwardsIsaby200846–47Purnell2011242–243Gimson2012178_179-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdwardsIsaby200846–47Purnell2011242–243Gimson2012178-179">&#91;175&#93;</a></sup> In his Shadow Cabinet reshuffle of May 2004, Howard appointed Johnson to the position of shadow arts minister.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011243Gimson2012179_180-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011243Gimson2012179-180">&#91;176&#93;</a></sup> In October, Howard ordered Johnson to apologise publicly in <a href="/wiki/Liverpool" title="Liverpool">Liverpool</a> for publishing a <i>Spectator</i> article – anonymously written by <a href="/wiki/Simon_Heffer" title="Simon Heffer">Simon Heffer</a> – which said the crowds at the <a href="/wiki/Hillsborough_disaster" title="Hillsborough disaster">Hillsborough disaster</a> had contributed towards the incident and that Liverpudlians had a predilection for reliance on the <a href="/wiki/Welfare_state_in_the_United_Kingdom" title="Welfare state in the United Kingdom">welfare state</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEEdwardsIsaby200847Purnell2011251–252Gimson2012193–207_181-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdwardsIsaby200847Purnell2011251–252Gimson2012193–207-181">&#91;177&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-182" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-182">&#91;178&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In November 2004, tabloids revealed that since 2000 Johnson had been having an affair with <i>Spectator</i> columnist <a href="/wiki/Petronella_Wyatt" title="Petronella Wyatt">Petronella Wyatt</a>, resulting in two <a href="/wiki/Abortion" title="Abortion">abortions</a>. Johnson initially called the claims "an inverted pyramid of piffle".<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEEdwardsIsaby200847Purnell2011257–263Gimson2012162–173,_209–218_183-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdwardsIsaby200847Purnell2011257–263Gimson2012162–173,_209–218-183">&#91;179&#93;</a></sup> After the allegations were proven, Howard asked Johnson to resign as vice-chairman and shadow arts minister for publicly lying; when Johnson refused, Howard dismissed him from those positions.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEEdwardsIsaby200847Purnell2011265–267Gimson2012222–223_184-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdwardsIsaby200847Purnell2011265–267Gimson2012222–223-184">&#91;180&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-185" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-185">&#91;181&#93;</a></sup> In July 2005, <i>Who's the Daddy?</i>, a play by <i>The Spectator</i><span class="nowrap" style="padding-left:0.1em;">&#39;</span>s theatre critics <a href="/wiki/Toby_Young" title="Toby Young">Toby Young</a> and Lloyd Evans being performed at Islington's <a href="/wiki/King%27s_Head_Theatre" title="King&#39;s Head Theatre">King's Head Theatre</a>, satirised the scandal.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011277–281Gimson2012232–233_186-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011277–281Gimson2012232–233-186">&#91;182&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="Second_term">Second term</span></h4>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-right" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:University_Park_MMB_21_Portland_Building_-_Boris_Johnson.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9b/University_Park_MMB_21_Portland_Building_-_Boris_Johnson.jpg/220px-University_Park_MMB_21_Portland_Building_-_Boris_Johnson.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="165" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9b/University_Park_MMB_21_Portland_Building_-_Boris_Johnson.jpg/330px-University_Park_MMB_21_Portland_Building_-_Boris_Johnson.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9b/University_Park_MMB_21_Portland_Building_-_Boris_Johnson.jpg/440px-University_Park_MMB_21_Portland_Building_-_Boris_Johnson.jpg 2x" data-file-width="1600" data-file-height="1200" /></a><figcaption>As Shadow Minister for Higher Education, Johnson visited various universities (as here at the <a href="/wiki/University_of_Nottingham" title="University of Nottingham">University of Nottingham</a> in 2006)</figcaption></figure>
