<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Boris_Johnson_cropped.JPG" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c2/Boris_Johnson_cropped.JPG/220px-Boris_Johnson_cropped.JPG" decoding="async" width="220" height="220" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c2/Boris_Johnson_cropped.JPG/330px-Boris_Johnson_cropped.JPG 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c2/Boris_Johnson_cropped.JPG/440px-Boris_Johnson_cropped.JPG 2x" data-file-width="492" data-file-height="491" /></a><figcaption>Johnson in 2007</figcaption></figure>
<p>At the <a href="/wiki/2005_United_Kingdom_general_election" title="2005 United Kingdom general election">2005 general election</a>, Johnson was re-elected MP for Henley, increasing his majority to 12,793.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011277Gimson2012232_187-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011277Gimson2012232-187">&#91;183&#93;</a></sup> Labour won the election and Howard stood down as Conservative leader; Johnson backed <a href="/wiki/David_Cameron" title="David Cameron">David Cameron</a> as his successor.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011283–284Gimson2012235–236_188-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011283–284Gimson2012235–236-188">&#91;184&#93;</a></sup> After Cameron was elected, he appointed Johnson as the shadow higher education minister, acknowledging his popularity among students.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEEdwardsIsaby200847Purnell2011289Gimson2012243_189-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdwardsIsaby200847Purnell2011289Gimson2012243-189">&#91;185&#93;</a></sup> Interested in streamlining university funding,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011302_190-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011302-190">&#91;186&#93;</a></sup> Johnson supported Labour's <a href="/wiki/Tuition_fees_in_the_United_Kingdom" title="Tuition fees in the United Kingdom">proposed top-up fees</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011291_191-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011291-191">&#91;187&#93;</a></sup> He campaigned in 2006 to become the <a href="/wiki/Rector_of_the_University_of_Edinburgh" title="Rector of the University of Edinburgh">Rector of the University of Edinburgh</a>, but his support for top-up fees damaged his campaign, and he came third.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011291–292Gimson2012248_192-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011291–292Gimson2012248-192">&#91;188&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-HES24Feb06_193-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-HES24Feb06-193">&#91;189&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In April 2006, the <i><a href="/wiki/News_of_the_World" title="News of the World">News of the World</a></i> alleged that Johnson was having an affair with the journalist Anna Fazackerley; the pair did not comment, and shortly afterwards Johnson began employing Fazackerley.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011296–300Gimson2012255–257_194-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011296–300Gimson2012255–257-194">&#91;190&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-auto_195-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-auto-195">&#91;191&#93;</a></sup> That month, he attracted further public attention for rugby-tackling former footballer <a href="/wiki/Maurizio_Gaudino" title="Maurizio Gaudino">Maurizio Gaudino</a> in a charity football match.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEGimson2012260_196-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGimson2012260-196">&#91;192&#93;</a></sup> In September 2006, Papua New Guinea's <a href="/wiki/High_Commission" class="mw-redirect" title="High Commission">High Commission</a> protested after he compared the Conservatives' frequently changing leadership to <a href="/wiki/Cannibalism#New_Guinea" title="Cannibalism">cannibalism in the country</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEGimson2012266_197-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGimson2012266-197">&#91;193&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In 2005, <i>The Spectator</i><span class="nowrap" style="padding-left:0.1em;">&#39;</span>s new chief executive, <a href="/wiki/Andrew_Neil" title="Andrew Neil">Andrew Neil</a>, dismissed Johnson as editor.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011289–290Gimson2012244–245_198-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011289–290Gimson2012244–245-198">&#91;194&#93;</a></sup> To make up for this loss of income, Johnson negotiated with <i>The Daily Telegraph</i> to raise his annual fee from £200,000 to £250,000, averaging at £5,000 per column, each of which took up around 90 minutes of his time.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011294–295_199-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011294–295-199">&#91;195&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-200" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-200">&#91;196&#93;</a></sup> He presented a <a href="/wiki/Popular_history" title="Popular history">popular history</a> television show, <i><a href="/wiki/The_Dream_of_Rome" title="The Dream of Rome">The Dream of Rome</a></i>, which was broadcast in January 2006; a book followed in February.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011292–293Gimson2012250–253_201-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011292–293Gimson2012250–253-201">&#91;197&#93;</a></sup> A sequel, <i>After Rome</i>, focused on early Islamic history.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011294_202-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011294-202">&#91;198&#93;</a></sup> As a result of his various activities, in 2007, he earned £540,000, making him the third-highest-earning MP that year.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011295_203-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011295-203">&#91;199&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h2><span id="Mayor_of_London_.282008.E2.80.932016.29"></span><span class="mw-headline" id="Mayor_of_London_(2008–2016)">Mayor of London (2008–2016)</span></h2>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Mayoralty_of_Boris_Johnson" title="Mayoralty of Boris Johnson">Mayoralty of Boris Johnson</a></div>
<h3><span id="Mayoral_election:_2007.E2.80.932008"></span><span class="mw-headline" id="Mayoral_election:_2007–2008">Mayoral election: 2007–2008</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/2008_London_mayoral_election" title="2008 London mayoral election">2008 London mayoral election</a></div>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">See also: <a href="/wiki/2007_London_Conservative_Party_mayoral_selection" title="2007 London Conservative Party mayoral selection">2007 London Conservative Party mayoral selection</a></div>
<p>In July 2007, Johnson announced his candidacy to be the Conservative candidate for <a href="/wiki/Mayor_of_London" title="Mayor of London">Mayor of London</a> in the 2008 mayoral election.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEEdwardsIsaby200852Purnell2011312Gimson2012278–279_204-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdwardsIsaby200852Purnell2011312Gimson2012278–279-204">&#91;200&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-205" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-205">&#91;201&#93;</a></sup> In September, he was selected after gaining 79 per cent of the vote in a public London-wide <a href="/wiki/Primary_election" title="Primary election">primary</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEEdwardsIsaby200853Gimson2012279_206-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdwardsIsaby200853Gimson2012279-206">&#91;202&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-207" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-207">&#91;203&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-right" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Boris_Johnson_-holding_a_red_model_bus_-2007.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/37/Boris_Johnson_-holding_a_red_model_bus_-2007.jpg/220px-Boris_Johnson_-holding_a_red_model_bus_-2007.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="180" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/37/Boris_Johnson_-holding_a_red_model_bus_-2007.jpg/330px-Boris_Johnson_-holding_a_red_model_bus_-2007.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/37/Boris_Johnson_-holding_a_red_model_bus_-2007.jpg/440px-Boris_Johnson_-holding_a_red_model_bus_-2007.jpg 2x" data-file-width="2061" data-file-height="1689" /></a><figcaption>Johnson pledged to replace the city's <a href="/wiki/Articulated_buses_in_London" title="Articulated buses in London">articulated buses</a> with <a href="/wiki/New_Routemaster" title="New Routemaster">New Routemaster</a> buses if elected mayor</figcaption></figure>
<p>Johnson's mayoral campaign focused on reducing youth crime, making public transport safer, and replacing the <a href="/wiki/Articulated_buses_in_London" title="Articulated buses in London">articulated buses</a> with an updated version of the <a href="/wiki/AEC_Routemaster" title="AEC Routemaster">AEC Routemaster</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011327_11-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011327-11">&#91;9&#93;</a></sup> Targeting the Conservative-leaning suburbs of <a href="/wiki/Outer_London" title="Outer London">outer London</a>, it capitalised on perceptions that the Labour Mayoralty had neglected them in favour of <a href="/wiki/Inner_London" title="Inner London">inner London</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011327Gimson2012285_208-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011327Gimson2012285-208">&#91;204&#93;</a></sup> His campaign emphasised his popularity, even among those who opposed his policies,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011326–327_209-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011326–327-209">&#91;205&#93;</a></sup> with opponents complaining a common attitude among voters was: "I'm voting for Boris because he is a laugh."<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011327_11-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011327-11">&#91;9&#93;</a></sup> The campaign of Labour incumbent <a href="/wiki/Ken_Livingstone" title="Ken Livingstone">Ken Livingstone</a> portrayed Johnson as an out-of-touch <a href="/wiki/Toff" title="Toff">toff</a> and bigot, citing alleged racist and homophobic language used in his columns; Johnson responded these quotes had been taken out of context and were intended as satire.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEHosken2008426–427EdwardsIsaby200867–69,_133Purnell201190,_315_210-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHosken2008426–427EdwardsIsaby200867–69,_133Purnell201190,_315-210">&#91;206&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In the election, Johnson received 43 per cent and Livingstone 37 per cent of first-preference votes; when second-preference votes were added, Johnson was victorious with 53 per cent to Livingstone's 47 per cent.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEEdwardsIsaby2008200–201Purnell2011348_211-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdwardsIsaby2008200–201Purnell2011348-211">&#91;207&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-bbcmayorwin_212-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-bbcmayorwin-212">&#91;208&#93;</a></sup> Johnson subsequently announced his intention to stand down as MP for Henley.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011351_213-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011351-213">&#91;209&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-214" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-214">&#91;210&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span id="First_term:_2008.E2.80.932012"></span><span class="mw-headline" id="First_term:_2008–2012">First term: 2008–2012</span></h3>
<p>After Johnson became mayor, those in City Hall who were deemed too closely allied to Livingstone's administration had their employment terminated.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011366_215-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011366-215">&#91;211&#93;</a></sup> Johnson appointed <a href="/wiki/Tim_Parker_(businessman)" title="Tim Parker (businessman)">Tim Parker</a> to be first Deputy Mayor, but after Parker began taking increasing control at City Hall and insisted that all staff report directly to him, Johnson dismissed him.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011368–271_216-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011368–271-216">&#91;212&#93;</a></sup> Because of these issues, many in the Conservative Party initially distanced themselves from Johnson's administration, fearing it would be counterproductive to achieving a Conservative victory at the <a href="/wiki/2010_United_Kingdom_general_election" title="2010 United Kingdom general election">2010 general election</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011368_217-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011368-217">&#91;213&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-right" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Boris_Johnson_on_the_podium.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c1/Boris_Johnson_on_the_podium.jpg/220px-Boris_Johnson_on_the_podium.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="165" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c1/Boris_Johnson_on_the_podium.jpg/330px-Boris_Johnson_on_the_podium.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c1/Boris_Johnson_on_the_podium.jpg/440px-Boris_Johnson_on_the_podium.jpg 2x" data-file-width="2272" data-file-height="1704" /></a><figcaption>Johnson gave a victory speech in <a href="/wiki/City_Hall,_Southwark" class="mw-redirect" title="City Hall, Southwark">City Hall</a> after being elected as the <a href="/wiki/Mayor_of_London" title="Mayor of London">Mayor of London</a></figcaption></figure>
<p>During the electoral campaign, Johnson had confided to <a href="/wiki/Brian_Paddick" class="mw-redirect" title="Brian Paddick">Brian Paddick</a> he was unsure how he would maintain his lifestyle while relying upon the mayoral salary of £140,000 a year.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011360_218-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011360-218">&#91;214&#93;</a></sup> To resolve this problem, he agreed to continue his <i>Daily Telegraph</i> column alongside his mayoral job, thus earning a further £250,000 a year.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011361_219-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011361-219">&#91;215&#93;</a></sup> His team believed this would cause controversy and made him promise to donate a fifth of his <i>Daily Telegraph</i> fee to a charitable cause providing bursaries for students. Johnson resented this, and ultimately did not pay a full fifth.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011362_220-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011362-220">&#91;216&#93;</a></sup> Controversy erupted when he was questioned about his <i>Daily Telegraph</i> fee on <a href="/wiki/BBC" title="BBC">BBC</a>'s <i><a href="/wiki/HARDtalk" title="HARDtalk">HARDtalk</a></i>; there, he referred to the £250,000 salary as "chicken feed", something that was widely condemned, given that this was then approximately 10 times the average yearly wage for a British worker.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011363_221-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011363-221">&#91;217&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-222" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-222">&#91;218&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-223" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-223">&#91;219&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Boris_Johnson_-opening_bell_at_NASDAQ-14Sept2009-3c.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1c/Boris_Johnson_-opening_bell_at_NASDAQ-14Sept2009-3c.jpg/220px-Boris_Johnson_-opening_bell_at_NASDAQ-14Sept2009-3c.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="178" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1c/Boris_Johnson_-opening_bell_at_NASDAQ-14Sept2009-3c.jpg/330px-Boris_Johnson_-opening_bell_at_NASDAQ-14Sept2009-3c.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1c/Boris_Johnson_-opening_bell_at_NASDAQ-14Sept2009-3c.jpg/440px-Boris_Johnson_-opening_bell_at_NASDAQ-14Sept2009-3c.jpg 2x" data-file-width="1236" data-file-height="1000" /></a><figcaption>Johnson at the opening of NASDAQ in 2009</figcaption></figure>
<p>During his first administration, Johnson was embroiled in several personal scandals. After moving to a new house in Islington, he built a shed on his balcony without obtaining <a href="/wiki/Planning_permission" title="Planning permission">planning permission</a>; after neighbours complained, he dismantled it.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011396–397Gimson2012308_224-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011396–397Gimson2012308-224">&#91;220&#93;</a></sup> The press also accused him of having an affair with Helen Macintyre and of fathering her child, allegations that he did not deny.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011407–410Gimson2012330–331_225-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011407–410Gimson2012330–331-225">&#91;221&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-theguardian2_226-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-theguardian2-226">&#91;222&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-227" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-227">&#91;223&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-Telegraph210513_228-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Telegraph210513-228">&#91;224&#93;</a></sup> Controversy arose when Johnson was accused of warning the MP <a href="/wiki/Damian_Green" title="Damian Green">Damian Green</a> that police were planning to arrest him; Johnson denied the claims and did not face criminal charges under the <a href="/wiki/Criminal_Justice_Act" title="Criminal Justice Act">Criminal Justice Act</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011380–385Gimson2012305–308_229-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011380–385Gimson2012305–308-229">&#91;225&#93;</a></sup> He was accused of <a href="/wiki/Cronyism" title="Cronyism">cronyism</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011407_230-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011407-230">&#91;226&#93;</a></sup> in particular for appointing <a href="/wiki/Veronica_Wadley" class="mw-redirect" title="Veronica Wadley">Veronica Wadley</a>, a former <i>Evening Standard</i> editor who had supported him, as the chair of London's <a href="/wiki/Arts_Council" class="mw-redirect" title="Arts Council">Arts Council</a> when she was widely regarded as not being the best candidate for the position.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011401–402_231-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011401–402-231">&#91;227&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-232" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-232">&#91;228&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-233" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-233">&#91;229&#93;</a></sup> He was implicated in the <a href="/wiki/United_Kingdom_parliamentary_expenses_scandal" title="United Kingdom parliamentary expenses scandal">parliamentary expenses scandal</a>, being accused of excessive expenses claims for taxis. His deputy mayor <a href="/wiki/Ian_Clement" title="Ian Clement">Ian Clement</a> was found to have misused a City Hall credit card, resulting in his resignation.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011392–395_234-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011392–395-234">&#91;230&#93;</a></sup>
Johnson remained a popular figure in London with a strong celebrity status.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011446_235-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011446-235">&#91;231&#93;</a></sup> In 2009, he rescued <a href="/wiki/Franny_Armstrong" title="Franny Armstrong">Franny Armstrong</a> from anti-social teenagers who had threatened her while he was cycling past them.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEGimson2012308_236-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGimson2012308-236">&#91;232&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-237" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-237">&#91;233&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-238" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-238">&#91;234&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="Policies">Policies</span></h4>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-right" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Arriva_London_bus_LT2_(LT61_BHT)_2011_New_Bus_for_London,_Victoria_bus_station,_route_38,_27_February_2012_(1).jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b7/Arriva_London_bus_LT2_%28LT61_BHT%29_2011_New_Bus_for_London%2C_Victoria_bus_station%2C_route_38%2C_27_February_2012_%281%29.jpg/220px-Arriva_London_bus_LT2_%28LT61_BHT%29_2011_New_Bus_for_London%2C_Victoria_bus_station%2C_route_38%2C_27_February_2012_%281%29.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="217" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b7/Arriva_London_bus_LT2_%28LT61_BHT%29_2011_New_Bus_for_London%2C_Victoria_bus_station%2C_route_38%2C_27_February_2012_%281%29.jpg/330px-Arriva_London_bus_LT2_%28LT61_BHT%29_2011_New_Bus_for_London%2C_Victoria_bus_station%2C_route_38%2C_27_February_2012_%281%29.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b7/Arriva_London_bus_LT2_%28LT61_BHT%29_2011_New_Bus_for_London%2C_Victoria_bus_station%2C_route_38%2C_27_February_2012_%281%29.jpg/440px-Arriva_London_bus_LT2_%28LT61_BHT%29_2011_New_Bus_for_London%2C_Victoria_bus_station%2C_route_38%2C_27_February_2012_%281%29.jpg 2x" data-file-width="2120" data-file-height="2095" /></a><figcaption>The <a href="/wiki/New_Routemaster" title="New Routemaster">New Routemaster</a> bus introduced by Johnson's administration</figcaption></figure>
<p>Johnson made no major changes to the mayoral system Livingstone developed.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011373_239-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011373-239">&#91;235&#93;</a></sup> He reversed several measures implemented by Livingstone's administration, ending the city's oil deal with Venezuela, abolishing <i><a href="/wiki/The_Londoner" title="The Londoner">The Londoner</a></i> newsletter, and scrapping the half-yearly inspections of <a href="/wiki/Hackney_carriage" title="Hackney carriage">black cabs</a>, which was reinstated three years later.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEEdwardsIsaby2008211Purnell2011373_240-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdwardsIsaby2008211Purnell2011373-240">&#91;236&#93;</a></sup> Abolishing the western wing of the <a href="/wiki/London_congestion_charge" title="London congestion charge">congestion charging</a> zone,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011443_241-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011443-241">&#91;237&#93;</a></sup> he cancelled plans to increase the congestion charge for <a href="/wiki/Four-wheel_drive" title="Four-wheel drive">four-wheel-drive vehicles</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011391_242-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011391-242">&#91;238&#93;</a></sup> He was subsequently accused of failing to publish an independent report on air pollution commissioned by the <a href="/wiki/Greater_London_Authority" title="Greater London Authority">Greater London Authority</a>, which revealed the city breached legal limits on <a href="/wiki/Nitrogen_dioxide" title="Nitrogen dioxide">nitrogen dioxide</a> levels.<sup id="cite_ref-tele_243-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-tele-243">&#91;239&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-244" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-244">&#91;240&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Johnson retained Livingstone projects such as <a href="/wiki/Crossrail" title="Crossrail">Crossrail</a> and the <a href="/wiki/2012_Summer_Olympics" title="2012 Summer Olympics">2012 Olympic Games</a>, but was accused of trying to take credit for them.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011390_245-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011390-245">&#91;241&#93;</a></sup> He introduced a public bicycle scheme that had been mooted by Livingstone's administration; colloquially known as "<a href="/wiki/Santander_Cycles" title="Santander Cycles">Boris Bikes</a>", the part privately financed system cost £140&#160;million and was a significant financial loss but proved popular.<sup id="cite_ref-246" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-246">&#91;242&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011414–416Gimson2012307_247-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011414–416Gimson2012307-247">&#91;243&#93;</a></sup> Despite Johnson's support of cycling in London, and his much-publicised identity as a cyclist, some cycling groups who argued he had failed to make the city's roads safer for cyclists criticised his administration.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011442–443_248-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011442–443-248">&#91;244&#93;</a></sup> As per his election pledge, he commissioned the development of the <a href="/wiki/New_Routemaster" title="New Routemaster">New Routemaster</a> buses for central London.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011417Gimson2012307_249-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011417Gimson2012307-249">&#91;245&#93;</a></sup> He also ordered the construction of a <a href="/wiki/Emirates_Air_Line_(cable_car)" class="mw-redirect" title="Emirates Air Line (cable car)">cable car system</a> that crossed the <a href="/wiki/River_Thames" title="River Thames">River Thames</a> between <a href="/wiki/Greenwich_Peninsula" title="Greenwich Peninsula">Greenwich Peninsula</a> and the <a href="/wiki/Royal_Docks" title="Royal Docks">Royal Docks</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011417–418_250-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011417–418-250">&#91;246&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-left" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:BorisBikes.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/46/BorisBikes.jpg/220px-BorisBikes.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="175" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/46/BorisBikes.jpg/330px-BorisBikes.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/46/BorisBikes.jpg/440px-BorisBikes.jpg 2x" data-file-width="602" data-file-height="480" /></a><figcaption>Johnson implemented Livingstone's idea of a public bicycle system; the result was dubbed the <a href="/wiki/Santander_Cycles" title="Santander Cycles">"Boris Bike"</a>.</figcaption></figure>
<p>Johnson's first policy initiative was a ban on drinking alcohol on public transport.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011265Gimson2012288_251-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011265Gimson2012288-251">&#91;247&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-lgovpr20080507_252-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-lgovpr20080507-252">&#91;248&#93;</a></sup> At the beginning of his tenure as mayor, Johnson announced plans to extend pay-as-you-go <a href="/wiki/Oyster_cards" class="mw-redirect" title="Oyster cards">Oyster cards</a> to national rail services in London.<sup id="cite_ref-es_oystersie_253-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-es_oystersie-253">&#91;249&#93;</a></sup> A pledge in Johnson's election manifesto was to retain Tube ticket offices, in opposition to Livingstone's proposal to close up to 40 London Underground ticket offices.<sup id="cite_ref-2008_transport_manifesto_254-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-2008_transport_manifesto-254">&#91;250&#93;</a></sup> On 2&#160;July 2008, the Mayor's office announced the closure plan was to be abandoned and that offices would remain open.<sup id="cite_ref-es_kenplan_255-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-es_kenplan-255">&#91;251&#93;</a></sup> On 21&#160;November 2013, <a href="/wiki/Transport_for_London" title="Transport for London">Transport for London</a> announced that all London Underground ticket offices would close by 2015.<sup id="cite_ref-bbc_borisplan_256-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-bbc_borisplan-256">&#91;252&#93;</a></sup> In financing these projects, Johnson's administration borrowed £100&#160;million,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011437_257-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011437-257">&#91;253&#93;</a></sup> while public transport fares were increased by 50 per cent.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011416_258-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011416-258">&#91;254&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>During his first Mayoral term, Johnson was perceived as having moved leftward on certain issues, for instance, supporting the <a href="/wiki/Living_wage_in_the_United_Kingdom" class="mw-redirect" title="Living wage in the United Kingdom">London Living Wage</a> and endorsing an amnesty for illegal migrants.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011388_259-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011388-259">&#91;255&#93;</a></sup> He tried placating critics who had deemed him a bigot by appearing at <a href="/wiki/Pride_London" class="mw-redirect" title="Pride London">London's gay pride parade</a> and praising ethnic minority newspapers.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011374–375_260-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011374–375-260">&#91;256&#93;</a></sup> In 2012, he banned London buses from displaying the adverts of <a href="/wiki/Core_Issues_Trust" title="Core Issues Trust">Core Issues Trust</a>, a Christian group, which compared homosexuality to an illness.<sup id="cite_ref-261" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-261">&#91;257&#93;</a></sup> In August 2008, Johnson broke from the traditional protocol of those in public office not publicly commenting on other nations' elections by endorsing <a href="/wiki/Barack_Obama" title="Barack Obama">Barack Obama</a> for the <a href="/wiki/2008_United_States_presidential_election" title="2008 United States presidential election">presidency of the United States</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-262" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-262">&#91;258&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-263" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-263">&#91;259&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span id="Relations_with_police.2C_finance.2C_and_the_media"></span><span class="mw-headline" id="Relations_with_police,_finance,_and_the_media">Relations with police, finance, and the media</span></h4>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-right" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:2011_London_riots.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/38/2011_London_riots.jpg/220px-2011_London_riots.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="146" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/38/2011_London_riots.jpg/330px-2011_London_riots.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/38/2011_London_riots.jpg/440px-2011_London_riots.jpg 2x" data-file-width="3577" data-file-height="2376" /></a><figcaption>Johnson's response to the 2011 London riots was criticised</figcaption></figure>
<p>Johnson appointed himself chair of the <a href="/wiki/Metropolitan_Police_Authority" title="Metropolitan Police Authority">Metropolitan Police Authority</a> (MPA), and in October 2008 successfully pushed for the resignation of Metropolitan Police Commissioner <a href="/wiki/Ian_Blair" title="Ian Blair">Ian Blair</a> after the latter was criticised for allegedly handing contracts to friends and for his handling of the <a href="/wiki/Death_of_Jean_Charles_de_Menezes" class="mw-redirect" title="Death of Jean Charles de Menezes">death of Jean Charles de Menezes</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011377–278Gimson2012304_264-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011377–278Gimson2012304-264">&#91;260&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-265" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-265">&#91;261&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-266" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-266">&#91;262&#93;</a></sup> This earned Johnson great respect among Conservatives, who interpreted it as his first act of strength.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011379_267-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011379-267">&#91;263&#93;</a></sup> Johnson resigned as MPA chairman in January 2010,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011388_259-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011388-259">&#91;255&#93;</a></sup> but throughout his mayoralty was highly supportive of the Metropolitan Police, particularly during the controversy surrounding the <a href="/wiki/Death_of_Ian_Tomlinson" title="Death of Ian Tomlinson">death of Ian Tomlinson</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011387–388_268-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011387–388-268">&#91;264&#93;</a></sup> Overall crime in London fell during his administration, but his claim that serious youth crime had decreased proved to be false, and he acknowledged the error.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011436_269-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011436-269">&#91;265&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-270" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-270">&#91;266&#93;</a></sup> Similarly, his claim that Metropolitan Police numbers had increased was characterised as untrue,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011436_269-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011436-269">&#91;265&#93;</a></sup> but the fact-checkers at <a href="/wiki/Full_Fact" title="Full Fact">Full Fact</a> felt that both Johnson's and his critics' positions are defensible.<sup id="cite_ref-271" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-271">&#91;267&#93;</a></sup> He was criticised for his response to the <a href="/wiki/2011_England_riots" title="2011 England riots">2011 London riots</a>; holidaying with his family in <a href="/wiki/British_Columbia" title="British Columbia">British Columbia</a> when the rioting broke out, he did not return immediately to London, only doing so 48 hours after it had begun and addressing Londoners 60 hours thereafter. Upon visiting shopkeepers and residents affected by the riots in <a href="/wiki/Clapham" title="Clapham">Clapham</a>, elements within the crowds booed and jeered him.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011429–432Gimson2012333–335_272-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011429–432Gimson2012333–335-272">&#91;268&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-left" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:BorisOC2010.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2c/BorisOC2010.jpg/220px-BorisOC2010.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="146" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2c/BorisOC2010.jpg/330px-BorisOC2010.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2c/BorisOC2010.jpg/440px-BorisOC2010.jpg 2x" data-file-width="4288" data-file-height="2848" /></a><figcaption>Johnson lights the flame at the 2010 <a href="/wiki/London_Youth_Games" title="London Youth Games">London Youth Games</a> opening ceremony</figcaption></figure>
<p>Johnson championed London's financial sector and denounced what he saw as "banker bashing" following the <a href="/wiki/Financial_crisis_of_2007%E2%80%9308" class="mw-redirect" title="Financial crisis of 2007–08">financial crisis of 2007–08</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011400Gimson2012324_273-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011400Gimson2012324-273">&#91;269&#93;</a></sup> condemning the <a href="/wiki/Anti-capitalism" title="Anti-capitalism">anti-capitalist</a> <a href="/wiki/Occupy_London" title="Occupy London">Occupy London</a> movement that appeared in 2011.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011439–440_274-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011439–440-274">&#91;270&#93;</a></sup> He spent much time with those involved in the financial services and criticised the government's 50p tax rate for higher earners.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011400_275-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011400-275">&#91;271&#93;</a></sup> He collected donations from the city's wealthy for a charitable enterprise, the Mayor's Fund, which he had established to aid disadvantaged youths. It initially announced the fund would raise £100&#160;million, but by 2010 it had only spent £1.5&#160;million.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011414_276-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011414-276">&#91;272&#93;</a></sup> He also maintained extensive personal contacts throughout the British media,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011389_277-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011389-277">&#91;273&#93;</a></sup> which resulted in widespread favourable press coverage of his administration.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011389_277-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011389-277">&#91;273&#93;</a></sup> In turn he remained largely supportive of his friends in the media – among them <a href="/wiki/Rupert_Murdoch" title="Rupert Murdoch">Rupert Murdoch</a> – during the <a href="/wiki/News_International_phone_hacking_scandal" title="News International phone hacking scandal">News International phone hacking scandal</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011424–425_278-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011424–425-278">&#91;274&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="Re-election_campaign">Re-election campaign</span></h4>
<p>Up for re-election in 2012, Johnson again hired Crosby to orchestrate his campaign.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEGimson2012338_279-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGimson2012338-279">&#91;275&#93;</a></sup>
Before the election, Johnson published <i>Johnson's Life of London</i>, a work of popular history that the historian <a href="/wiki/A._N._Wilson" title="A. N. Wilson">A. N. Wilson</a> characterised as a "coded plea" for votes.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011447–448_280-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011447–448-280">&#91;276&#93;</a></sup>
Polls suggested that while Livingstone's approach to transport was preferred, voters in London placed greater trust in Johnson over issues of crime and the economy.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011440_281-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011440-281">&#91;277&#93;</a></sup> During the <a href="/wiki/2012_London_mayoral_election" title="2012 London mayoral election">2012 Mayoral election</a>, Johnson sought re-election, while Livingstone was selected as the Labour candidate again. Johnson's campaign emphasised the accusation that Livingstone was guilty of <a href="/wiki/Tax_evasion" title="Tax evasion">tax evasion</a>, for which Livingstone called Johnson a "bare-faced liar".<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECrines20133_282-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECrines20133-282">&#91;278&#93;</a></sup> The political scientist Andrew Crines believed that Livingstone's campaign focused on criticising Johnson rather than presenting an alternate and progressive vision of London's future.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECrines20132_283-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECrines20132-283">&#91;279&#93;</a></sup> In 2012, Johnson was <a href="/wiki/2012_London_mayoral_election" title="2012 London mayoral election">re-elected</a> as mayor.<sup id="cite_ref-BBC5May12_284-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-BBC5May12-284">&#91;280&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span id="Second_term:_2012.E2.80.932016"></span><span class="mw-headline" id="Second_term:_2012–2016">Second term: 2012–2016</span></h3>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-right" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Boris_2012.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1f/Boris_2012.jpg/220px-Boris_2012.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="146" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1f/Boris_2012.jpg/330px-Boris_2012.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1f/Boris_2012.jpg/440px-Boris_2012.jpg 2x" data-file-width="4928" data-file-height="3264" /></a><figcaption>Johnson at the <a href="/wiki/2012_Summer_Olympics" title="2012 Summer Olympics">2012 Summer Olympics</a></figcaption></figure>
<p>London was successful in its bid to host the <a href="/wiki/2012_Summer_Olympics" title="2012 Summer Olympics">2012 Summer Olympics</a> while Ken Livingstone was still mayor in 2005. Johnson's role in the proceedings was as the co-chair of an Olympic board which oversaw the games.<sup id="cite_ref-285" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-285">&#91;281&#93;</a></sup> Two of his actions after taking on this role were to improve transportation around London by making more tickets available and laying on more buses around the capital during the busy period, when thousands of spectators were temporary visitors in London.<sup id="cite_ref-286" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-286">&#91;282&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-287" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-287">&#91;283&#93;</a></sup> Johnson was accused of covering up pollution ahead of the games by deploying dust suppressants to remove air particulates near monitoring stations.<sup id="cite_ref-tele_243-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-tele-243">&#91;239&#93;</a></sup> In November 2013, Johnson announced major changes to the operation of <a href="/wiki/London_Underground" title="London Underground">London Underground</a>, including the extension of operating hours to run through the night at weekends. All staffed ticket offices would be closed to save over £40&#160;million a year and replaced with automated ticketing systems.<sup id="cite_ref-bbc_tube_ticket_288-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-bbc_tube_ticket-288">&#91;284&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-es_shakeup_289-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-es_shakeup-289">&#91;285&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Johnson had a close friendship with American technology entrepreneur, former DJ<sup id="cite_ref-290" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-290">&#91;286&#93;</a></sup> and model <a href="/wiki/Jennifer_Arcuri" title="Jennifer Arcuri">Jennifer Arcuri</a>, with <i><a href="/wiki/The_Sunday_Times" title="The Sunday Times">The Sunday Times</a></i> describing him as a regular visitor to her flat,<sup id="cite_ref-291" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-291">&#91;287&#93;</a></sup> and implying they were in a sexual relationship.<sup id="cite_ref-sky_292-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-sky-292">&#91;288&#93;</a></sup> In 2013, a mayoral fund awarded her company, Innotech, £10,000, followed the next year by Arcuri being awarded £15,000 from a government programme. Johnson intervened to allow her onto three trade mission trips.<sup id="cite_ref-293" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-293">&#91;289&#93;</a></sup> <i>The Sunday Times</i> said in September 2019 that Johnson failed to declare his personal relationship as a conflict of interest.<sup id="cite_ref-294" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-294">&#91;290&#93;</a></sup> Later that month, the Greater London Authority referred Johnson and his actions in the matter to the <a href="/wiki/Independent_Office_for_Police_Conduct" title="Independent Office for Police Conduct">Independent Office for Police Conduct</a> (IOPC) "so it can assess whether or not it is necessary to investigate the former mayor of London for the criminal offence of misconduct in public office". The IOPC was involved because the Mayor is also London's <a href="/wiki/Police_and_crime_commissioner" title="Police and crime commissioner">police and crime commissioner</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-295" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-295">&#91;291&#93;</a></sup> The <a href="/wiki/London_Assembly" title="London Assembly">London Assembly</a> began its own investigation but paused it at the IOPC's request to avoid overlap. On 9&#160;November 2019 it was revealed that the IOPC, which had been due to publish a report on its investigation, had decided to do so after the general election of 12&#160;December.<sup id="cite_ref-296" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-296">&#91;292&#93;</a></sup> The IOPC issued its report in May 2020, concluding that, although there was no basis for any criminal charge, there was evidence that the close relationship between Johnson and Arcuri had influenced decisions by officials. The report found Johnson should have declared an interest concerning Arcuri and that his failure to do this could have breached the London Assembly's code of conduct. On behalf of the London Assembly, the chair of its Greater London Authority Oversight Committee said the committee would now resume its own investigation.<sup id="cite_ref-297" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-297">&#91;293&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In 2015, Johnson criticised then-presidential candidate <a href="/wiki/Donald_Trump" title="Donald Trump">Donald Trump</a>'s false comments that there were <a href="/wiki/No-go_area#United_Kingdom" title="No-go area">no-go zones in London</a> governed by <a href="/wiki/Shariah" class="mw-redirect" title="Shariah">shariah</a> and inaccessible for non-Muslims. Johnson said Trump was "betraying a quite stupefying ignorance that makes him, frankly, unfit to hold the office of president of the United States",<sup id="cite_ref-Waugh_298-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Waugh-298">&#91;294&#93;</a></sup> becoming the first senior politician in the UK to declare Trump unfit for office, but rejecting calls for him to be banned from the country.<sup id="cite_ref-299" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-299">&#91;295&#93;</a></sup> Johnson added that he "would invite [Trump] to come and see the whole of London and take him round the city – except I wouldn't want to expose Londoners to any unnecessary risk of meeting Donald Trump".<sup id="cite_ref-Waugh_298-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Waugh-298">&#91;294&#93;</a></sup> He later called Trump's comments "ill informed" and "complete and utter nonsense", adding that "the only reason I wouldn't go to some parts of New York is the real risk of meeting Donald Trump".<sup id="cite_ref-300" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-300">&#91;296&#93;</a></sup> In 2016, he said he was "genuinely worried that he could become president", telling ITV's <a href="/wiki/Tom_Bradby" title="Tom Bradby">Tom Bradby</a> of one moment where he was mistaken for Trump in New York as "one of the worst moments" of his life.<sup id="cite_ref-Telegraph160321_301-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Telegraph160321-301">&#91;297&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Johnson did not run for a third term for Mayor of London and stepped down on 5&#160;May 2016 following <a href="/wiki/2016_London_mayoral_election" title="2016 London mayoral election">the election</a> of former transport minister, <a href="/wiki/Sadiq_Khan" title="Sadiq Khan">Sadiq Khan</a>. A <a href="/wiki/YouGov" title="YouGov">YouGov</a> poll commissioned at the end of Johnson's term revealed that 52% of Londoners believed he did a "good job" as Mayor of London while 29% believed he did a "bad job".<sup id="cite_ref-302" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-302">&#91;298&#93;</a></sup> In 2016, Sadiq Khan announced that three German-made water cannon, which Johnson had bought for the <a href="/wiki/Metropolitan_Police" title="Metropolitan Police">Metropolitan Police</a> without waiting for clearance from the then-Home Secretary <a href="/wiki/Theresa_May" title="Theresa May">Theresa May</a>, were to be sold, with the proceeds going to youth services.<sup id="cite_ref-303" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-303">&#91;299&#93;</a></sup> The vehicles proved unsellable and were eventually sold for scrap in 2018 at a £300,000 loss.<sup id="cite_ref-304" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-304">&#91;300&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h2><span class="mw-headline" id="Return_to_Parliament">Return to Parliament</span></h2>
<p>Johnson initially said that he would not return to the House of Commons while remaining mayor.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011446_235-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurnell2011446-235">&#91;231&#93;</a></sup> After much media speculation, in August 2014 he sought selection as the Conservative candidate for the <a href="/wiki/Safe_seat" title="Safe seat">safe seat</a> of <a href="/wiki/Uxbridge_and_South_Ruislip_(UK_Parliament_constituency)" title="Uxbridge and South Ruislip (UK Parliament constituency)">Uxbridge and South Ruislip</a> at the <a href="/wiki/2015_United_Kingdom_general_election" title="2015 United Kingdom general election">2015 general election</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-305" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-305">&#91;301&#93;</a></sup> becoming the party's candidate in September.<sup id="cite_ref-306" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-306">&#91;302&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-307" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-307">&#91;303&#93;</a></sup> In the <a href="/wiki/2015_United_Kingdom_general_election" title="2015 United Kingdom general election">2015 general election</a>, Johnson was elected MP. There was much speculation that he had returned to Parliament because he wanted to replace Cameron as Conservative leader and prime minister.<sup id="cite_ref-308" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-308">&#91;304&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span id="Brexit_campaign:_2015.E2.80.932016"></span><span class="mw-headline" id="Brexit_campaign:_2015–2016">Brexit campaign: 2015–2016</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Vote_Leave" title="Vote Leave">Vote Leave</a></div>
<p>In February 2016, Johnson endorsed <a href="/wiki/Vote_Leave" title="Vote Leave">Vote Leave</a> in the "Out" campaign for the <a href="/wiki/2016_United_Kingdom_European_Union_membership_referendum" title="2016 United Kingdom European Union membership referendum">2016 European Union membership referendum</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-309" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-309">&#91;305&#93;</a></sup> He called Cameron's warnings about leaving "greatly over exaggerated". Following this announcement, which was interpreted by financial markets as making Brexit more probable, the <a href="/wiki/Pound_sterling" title="Pound sterling">pound sterling</a> slumped by nearly 2% against the US dollar, reaching its lowest level since March 2009.<sup id="cite_ref-310" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-310">&#91;306&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In April 2016, in an article for <i><a href="/wiki/The_Sun_(United_Kingdom)" title="The Sun (United Kingdom)">The Sun</a></i>, in response to a comment by President <a href="/wiki/Barack_Obama" title="Barack Obama">Barack Obama</a> that Britain should remain in the European Union, Johnson said an "ancestral dislike" of Britain owing to his "part-Kenyan" background may have shaped Obama's views.<sup id="cite_ref-controversial_311-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-controversial-311">&#91;307&#93;</a></sup> Conservative MP Sir <a href="/wiki/Nicholas_Soames" title="Nicholas Soames">Nicholas Soames</a> branded the comments "idiotic" and "deeply offensive".<sup id="cite_ref-Obama_312-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Obama-312">&#91;308&#93;</a></sup> Several Labour and Liberal Democrat politicians condemned them as racist and unacceptable.<sup id="cite_ref-ObamaSmear_313-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-ObamaSmear-313">&#91;309&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-ToIApril16_314-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-ToIApril16-314">&#91;310&#93;</a></sup> In light of the remark, a <a href="/wiki/King%27s_College_London" title="King&#39;s College London">King's College London</a> student society revoked a speaking invitation it had extended to him.<sup id="cite_ref-315" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-315">&#91;311&#93;</a></sup> Conversely, former Conservative Party leader <a href="/wiki/Iain_Duncan_Smith" title="Iain Duncan Smith">Iain Duncan Smith</a> and <a href="/wiki/UK_Independence_Party" title="UK Independence Party">UK Independence Party</a> (UKIP) leader <a href="/wiki/Nigel_Farage" title="Nigel Farage">Nigel Farage</a> defended his comments.<sup id="cite_ref-ObamaSmear_313-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-ObamaSmear-313">&#91;309&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-316" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-316">&#91;312&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Johnson supported Vote Leave's statement that the government was committed to <a href="/wiki/Accession_of_Turkey_to_the_European_Union" title="Accession of Turkey to the European Union">Turkish accession to the EU</a> at the earliest possible opportunity, contradicting the Britain Stronger in Europe campaign's view that Turkey "is not an issue in this referendum and it shouldn't be". Vote Leave was accused of implying that 80&#160;million Turks would come to the UK if it stayed in the EU. When interviewed in January 2019, he said he had not mentioned Turkey during the campaign.<sup id="cite_ref-317" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-317">&#91;313&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-318" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-318">&#91;314&#93;</a></sup> On 22&#160;June 2016, Johnson declared 23&#160;June could be "Britain's independence day" in a televised debate in front of a 6,000-member audience at <a href="/wiki/Wembley_Arena" title="Wembley Arena">Wembley Arena</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-319" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-319">&#91;315&#93;</a></sup> <a href="/wiki/David_Cameron" title="David Cameron">David Cameron</a>, British prime minister at the time, specifically addressed Johnson's claim, publicly stating, "the idea that our country isn't independent is nonsense. This whole debate demonstrates our sovereignty."<sup id="cite_ref-320" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-320">&#91;316&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Following the victory of the "Leave" campaign, Cameron resigned as Conservative leader and prime minister. Johnson was widely regarded as the front-runner to succeed him.<sup id="cite_ref-321" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-321">&#91;317&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-322" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-322">&#91;318&#93;</a></sup> Johnson announced he would not stand in the <a href="/wiki/2016_Conservative_Party_leadership_election" title="2016 Conservative Party leadership election">Conservative leadership election</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-323" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-323">&#91;319&#93;</a></sup> Shortly before this, Michael Gove, hitherto a Johnson ally, concluded that Johnson "cannot provide the leadership or build the team for the task ahead".<sup id="cite_ref-324" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-324">&#91;320&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-325" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-325">&#91;321&#93;</a></sup> <i>The Daily Telegraph</i> called Gove's comments "the most spectacular political assassination in a generation".<sup id="cite_ref-326" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-326">&#91;322&#93;</a></sup> Johnson endorsed <a href="/wiki/Andrea_Leadsom" title="Andrea Leadsom">Andrea Leadsom</a>'s candidature, but she dropped out of the race a week later, leaving Theresa May to be elected uncontested.<sup id="cite_ref-327" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-327">&#91;323&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span id="Foreign_Secretary:_2016.E2.80.932018"></span><span class="mw-headline" id="Foreign_Secretary:_2016–2018">Foreign Secretary: 2016–2018</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Boris_Johnson%27s_tenure_as_Foreign_Secretary" title="Boris Johnson&#39;s tenure as Foreign Secretary">Boris Johnson's tenure as Foreign Secretary</a></div>
<figure typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Boris_johnson_(cropped).jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a8/Boris_johnson_%28cropped%29.jpg/193px-Boris_johnson_%28cropped%29.jpg" decoding="async" width="193" height="245" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a8/Boris_johnson_%28cropped%29.jpg/290px-Boris_johnson_%28cropped%29.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a8/Boris_johnson_%28cropped%29.jpg/386px-Boris_johnson_%28cropped%29.jpg 2x" data-file-width="504" data-file-height="640" /></a><figcaption>Official portrait of Johnson as Foreign Secretary</figcaption></figure>
<p>After May had become Conservative Party leader and prime minister, she appointed Johnson <a href="/wiki/Foreign_Secretary" title="Foreign Secretary">Foreign Secretary</a> in July 2016.<sup id="cite_ref-BloombergFSec_328-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-BloombergFSec-328">&#91;324&#93;</a></sup> Analysts saw the appointment as a tactic to weaken Johnson politically: the new positions of "<a href="/wiki/Brexit_secretary" class="mw-redirect" title="Brexit secretary">Brexit secretary</a>" and <a href="/wiki/Secretary_of_State_for_International_Trade" title="Secretary of State for International Trade">international trade secretary</a> left the foreign secretary as a figurehead with few powers.<sup id="cite_ref-BloombergFSec_328-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-BloombergFSec-328">&#91;324&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-GoodForMay_329-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-GoodForMay-329">&#91;325&#93;</a></sup> Johnson's appointment ensured he would often be out of the country and unable to organise and mobilise backbenchers against her, while forcing him to take responsibility for problems caused by withdrawing from the EU.<sup id="cite_ref-330" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-330">&#91;326&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-NewYorker_331-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-NewYorker-331">&#91;327&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>
Some journalists and foreign politicians criticised Johnson's appointment because of his history of controversial statements about other countries.<sup id="cite_ref-332" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-332">&#91;328&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FSecReactions_333-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FSecReactions-333">&#91;329&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-GuardianReactions_334-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-GuardianReactions-334">&#91;330&#93;</a></sup> His tenure in the role attracted criticism from diplomats and foreign policy experts.<sup id="cite_ref-bbc_335-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-bbc-335">&#91;331&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-theguardian3_336-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-theguardian3-336">&#91;332&#93;</a></sup> A number of diplomats, FCO staff and foreign ministers who worked with Johnson compared his leadership unfavourably to previous foreign secretaries for his perceived lack of conviction or substantive positions on British foreign policy issues.<sup id="cite_ref-bbc_335-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-bbc-335">&#91;331&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-theguardian3_336-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-theguardian3-336">&#91;332&#93;</a></sup> Former Swedish prime minister <a href="/wiki/Carl_Bildt" title="Carl Bildt">Carl Bildt</a> said: "I wish it was a joke."<sup id="cite_ref-337" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-337">&#91;333&#93;</a></sup> A senior official in Obama's government suggested Johnson's appointment would push the US further towards <a href="/wiki/Germany%E2%80%93United_States_relations" title="Germany–United States relations">Germany</a> at the expense of the <a href="/wiki/Special_Relationship" title="Special Relationship">Special Relationship</a> with the UK.<sup id="cite_ref-ITV20160714_338-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-ITV20160714-338">&#91;334&#93;</a></sup> On one occasion Egyptian president <a href="/wiki/Abdel_Fattah_el-Sisi" title="Abdel Fattah el-Sisi">Abdel Fattah el-Sisi</a> walked out of a meeting with Johnson after a meeting did not "get beyond the pleasantries".<sup id="cite_ref-bbc_335-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-bbc-335">&#91;331&#93;</a></sup></p><figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-left" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:President_Donald_J._Trump_and_the_British_Secretary_of_State_for_Foreign_and_Commonwealth_Affairs_Boris_Johnson_(37425398262).jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img decoding="async" width="220" height="165" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0e/President_Donald_J._Trump_and_the_British_Secretary_of_State_for_Foreign_and_Commonwealth_Affairs_Boris_Johnson_%2837425398262%29.jpg/330px-President_Donald_J._Trump_and_the_British_Secretary_of_State_for_Foreign_and_Commonwealth_Affairs_Boris_Johnson_%2837425398262%29.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0e/President_Donald_J._Trump_and_the_British_Secretary_of_State_for_Foreign_and_Commonwealth_Affairs_Boris_Johnson_%2837425398262%29.jpg/440px-President_Donald_J._Trump_and_the_British_Secretary_of_State_for_Foreign_and_Commonwealth_Affairs_Boris_Johnson_%2837425398262%29.jpg 2x" data-file-width="1728" data-file-height="1296" /></a><figcaption>Johnson with US president <a href="/wiki/Donald_Trump" title="Donald Trump">Donald Trump</a> in 2017 <a href="/wiki/UNGA" class="mw-redirect" title="UNGA">UNGA</a></figcaption></figure><p>Johnson's visit to Turkey from 25&#160;to 27&#160;September 2016 was somewhat tense because he had won <a href="/wiki/Douglas_Murray_(author)" title="Douglas Murray (author)">Douglas Murray</a>'s offensive poetry competition about the President of Turkey, <a href="/wiki/Recep_Tayyip_Erdo%C4%9Fan" title="Recep Tayyip Erdoğan">Recep Tayyip Erdoğan</a>, four months earlier.<sup id="cite_ref-339" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-339">&#91;335&#93;</a></sup> When questioned by a journalist whether he would apologise for the poem, Johnson dismissed the matter as "trivia".<sup id="cite_ref-340" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-340">&#91;336&#93;</a></sup> Johnson pledged to help <a href="/wiki/Accession_of_Turkey_to_the_European_Union" title="Accession of Turkey to the European Union">Turkey join the EU</a> and expressed support for Erdogan's government.<sup id="cite_ref-341" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-341">&#91;337&#93;</a></sup> 
</p><p>Johnson supported the <a href="/wiki/Saudi_Arabian%E2%80%93led_intervention_in_Yemen" class="mw-redirect" title="Saudi Arabian–led intervention in Yemen">Saudi Arabian–led intervention in Yemen</a> and refused to block UK arms sales to Saudi Arabia,<sup id="cite_ref-342" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-342">&#91;338&#93;</a></sup> stating there was no clear evidence of breaches of international humanitarian law by Saudi Arabia in the <a href="/wiki/Yemeni_Civil_War_(2014%E2%80%93present)" class="mw-redirect" title="Yemeni Civil War (2014–present)">war in Yemen</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-343" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-343">&#91;339&#93;</a></sup> In September 2016, human rights groups accused him of blocking the UN inquiry into Saudi war crimes in Yemen.<sup id="cite_ref-344" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-344">&#91;340&#93;</a></sup> Given the UK-Saudi alliance, in December 2016, he attracted attention for commenting the Saudis were akin to the Iranians in "puppeteering and playing <a href="/wiki/Iran%E2%80%93Saudi_Arabia_proxy_conflict" title="Iran–Saudi Arabia proxy conflict">proxy wars</a>" throughout the Middle East.<sup id="cite_ref-bbc.co.uk_345-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-bbc.co.uk-345">&#91;341&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-346" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-346">&#91;342&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-347" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-347">&#91;343&#93;</a></sup> May said his comments did not represent the government's view.<sup id="cite_ref-348" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-348">&#91;344&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>
In November 2017, Johnson told the <a href="/wiki/Foreign_Affairs_Select_Committee" title="Foreign Affairs Select Committee">Foreign Affairs Select Committee</a> that <a href="/wiki/Nazanin_Zaghari-Ratcliffe" title="Nazanin Zaghari-Ratcliffe">Nazanin Zaghari-Ratcliffe</a> – a British-Iranian dual citizen serving a five-year prison sentence in Iran after being arrested for training citizen journalists and bloggers in a <a href="/wiki/BBC_World_Service_Trust" class="mw-redirect" title="BBC World Service Trust">BBC World Service Trust</a> project – had been "simply teaching people journalism". Zaghari-Ratcliffe had said that her visit had been made simply for her daughter to meet her grandparents. Facing criticism, Johnson stated he had been misquoted and that nothing he said had justified Zaghari-Ratcliffe's sentence.<sup id="cite_ref-349" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-349">&#91;345&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-350" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-350">&#91;346&#93;</a></sup> In May 2018, Johnson backed<sup id="cite_ref-351" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-351">&#91;347&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-352" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-352">&#91;348&#93;</a></sup> the <a href="/wiki/Iran_nuclear_deal_framework" title="Iran nuclear deal framework">Iran nuclear deal framework</a>, despite Donald Trump's withdrawal.<sup id="cite_ref-353" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-353">&#91;349&#93;</a></sup> Johnson said the deal brought economic benefits to the Iranian people.<sup id="cite_ref-354" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-354">&#91;350&#93;</a></sup> Johnson described the <a href="/wiki/G%C3%BClen_movement" title="Gülen movement">Gülen movement</a> as a "cult" and supported <a href="/wiki/2016%E2%80%93present_purges_in_Turkey" title="2016–present purges in Turkey">Turkey's post-coup purges</a>. He said that <a href="/wiki/2016_Turkish_coup_d%27%C3%A9tat_attempt" class="mw-redirect" title="2016 Turkish coup d&#39;état attempt">Turkey's coup attempt</a> "was deeply violent, deeply anti-democratic, deeply sinister and it was totally right that it was crushed".<sup id="cite_ref-355" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-355">&#91;351&#93;</a></sup></p><figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Boris_Johnson_in_the_British_Virgin_Islands_after_Irma.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/96/Boris_Johnson_in_the_British_Virgin_Islands_after_Irma.jpg/220px-Boris_Johnson_in_the_British_Virgin_Islands_after_Irma.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="147" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/96/Boris_Johnson_in_the_British_Virgin_Islands_after_Irma.jpg/330px-Boris_Johnson_in_the_British_Virgin_Islands_after_Irma.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/96/Boris_Johnson_in_the_British_Virgin_Islands_after_Irma.jpg/440px-Boris_Johnson_in_the_British_Virgin_Islands_after_Irma.jpg 2x" data-file-width="960" data-file-height="640" /></a><figcaption>Johnson visiting the <a href="/wiki/British_Virgin_Islands" title="British Virgin Islands">British Virgin Islands</a> after <a href="/wiki/Hurricane_Irma" title="Hurricane Irma">Hurricane Irma</a></figcaption></figure><p>In April 2017, Johnson said that <a href="/wiki/Status_of_Gibraltar" title="Status of Gibraltar">Gibraltar's sovereignty</a> was "not going to change" after Brexit.<sup id="cite_ref-356" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-356">&#91;352&#93;</a></sup> Johnson promised while in <a href="/wiki/Northern_Ireland" title="Northern Ireland">Northern Ireland</a> that Brexit would leave the Irish border "absolutely unchanged".<sup id="cite_ref-357" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-357">&#91;353&#93;</a></sup> In May 2017, during the <a href="/wiki/2017_United_Kingdom_general_election" title="2017 United Kingdom general election">2017 United Kingdom general election</a>, a woman criticised him for discussing ending tariffs on Indian whisky in a <a href="/wiki/Gurdwara" title="Gurdwara">Sikh temple</a> in Bristol (<a href="/wiki/Prohibitions_in_Sikhism" title="Prohibitions in Sikhism">Sikhism prohibits alcohol use</a>). He later expressed regret that the protester held differing views to his on alcohol.<sup id="cite_ref-358" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-358">&#91;354&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Johnson visited the islands of <a href="/wiki/Anguilla" title="Anguilla">Anguilla</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Tortola" title="Tortola">Tortola</a> (in the <a href="/wiki/British_Virgin_Islands" title="British Virgin Islands">British Virgin Islands</a>) on 13&#160;September 2017 to confirm the United Kingdom's commitment to helping restore British territories devastated by <a href="/wiki/Hurricane_Irma" title="Hurricane Irma">Hurricane Irma</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-359" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-359">&#91;355&#93;</a></sup> He said he was reminded of photos of <a href="/wiki/Hiroshima" title="Hiroshima">Hiroshima</a> after the <a href="/wiki/Atom_bomb" class="mw-redirect" title="Atom bomb">atom bomb</a> had landed on it.<sup id="cite_ref-360" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-360">&#91;356&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In September 2017, he was criticised for reciting lines from <a href="/wiki/Rudyard_Kipling" title="Rudyard Kipling">Rudyard Kipling</a>'s poem <i><a href="/wiki/Mandalay_(poem)" title="Mandalay (poem)">Mandalay</a></i> while visiting a <a href="/wiki/Myanmar" title="Myanmar">Myanmar</a> temple; the British ambassador, who was with him, suggested it was "not appropriate".<sup id="cite_ref-361" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-361">&#91;357&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-362" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-362">&#91;358&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-363" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-363">&#91;359&#93;</a></sup> In October 2017, he faced criticism for stating the Libyan city of <a href="/wiki/Sirte" title="Sirte">Sirte</a> could become an economic success like <a href="/wiki/Dubai" title="Dubai">Dubai</a>: "all they have to do is clear the dead bodies away".<sup id="cite_ref-364" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-364">&#91;360&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-365" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-365">&#91;361&#93;</a></sup> Johnson did not condemn the actions of the Spanish government and police during the outlawed <a href="/wiki/2017_Catalan_independence_referendum" title="2017 Catalan independence referendum">Catalan independence referendum</a> on 1&#160;October 2017.<sup id="cite_ref-366" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-366">&#91;362&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Initially favouring a less hostile approach to Russia,<sup id="cite_ref-367" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-367">&#91;363&#93;</a></sup> Johnson soon backed a more aggressive policy towards Russia.<sup id="cite_ref-368" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-368">&#91;364&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-369" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-369">&#91;365&#93;</a></sup> Following the March 2018 <a href="/wiki/Poisoning_of_Sergei_and_Yulia_Skripal" title="Poisoning of Sergei and Yulia Skripal">poisoning of Sergei and Yulia Skripal</a> in <a href="/wiki/Salisbury" title="Salisbury">Salisbury</a>, an act which the UK government blamed on Russia,<sup id="cite_ref-370" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-370">&#91;366&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-371" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-371">&#91;367&#93;</a></sup> Johnson compared <a href="/wiki/Vladimir_Putin" title="Vladimir Putin">Vladimir Putin</a>'s hosting of the <a href="/wiki/2018_FIFA_World_Cup" title="2018 FIFA World Cup">World Cup in Russia</a> to <a href="/wiki/Adolf_Hitler" title="Adolf Hitler">Adolf Hitler</a>'s hosting of the <a href="/wiki/1936_Summer_Olympics" title="1936 Summer Olympics">Olympic Games in Berlin</a> in 1936.<sup id="cite_ref-372" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-372">&#91;368&#93;</a></sup> Russia's Foreign Ministry denounced Johnson's "unacceptable and unworthy" parallel towards Russia, a "nation that <a href="/wiki/World_War_II_casualties_of_the_Soviet_Union" title="World War II casualties of the Soviet Union">lost millions of lives</a> in fighting Nazism".<sup id="cite_ref-373" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-373">&#91;369&#93;</a></sup> Johnson described the <a href="/wiki/Nord_Stream_2" title="Nord Stream 2">Nord Stream&#160;2</a> gas pipeline from Russia to Germany as "divisive" and a "threat" that left Europe dependent on a "malign Russia" for its <a href="/wiki/Russia_in_the_European_energy_sector" title="Russia in the European energy sector">energy supplies</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-374" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-374">&#91;370&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Johnson condemned the <a href="/wiki/Rohingya_genocide" title="Rohingya genocide">persecution</a> of <a href="/wiki/Rohingya_Muslims" class="mw-redirect" title="Rohingya Muslims">Rohingya Muslims</a> in Myanmar,<sup id="cite_ref-375" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-375">&#91;371&#93;</a></sup> comparing the situation with the <a href="/wiki/Palestinian_refugees" title="Palestinian refugees">displacement of Palestinians</a> in 1948.<sup id="cite_ref-376" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-376">&#91;372&#93;</a></sup> Johnson supported the <a href="/wiki/Turkish_military_operation_in_Afrin" class="mw-redirect" title="Turkish military operation in Afrin">Turkish invasion of northern Syria</a> aimed at ousting the <a href="/wiki/People%27s_Protection_Units" class="mw-redirect" title="People&#39;s Protection Units">Syrian Kurds</a> from the enclave of <a href="/wiki/Afrin,_Syria" title="Afrin, Syria">Afrin</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-377" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-377">&#91;373&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-left" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Javad_Zarif_meeting_with_UK_foreign_minister_Boris_Johnson_in_Tehran_2017-12-09_02.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1e/Javad_Zarif_meeting_with_UK_foreign_minister_Boris_Johnson_in_Tehran_2017-12-09_02.jpg/220px-Javad_Zarif_meeting_with_UK_foreign_minister_Boris_Johnson_in_Tehran_2017-12-09_02.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="135" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1e/Javad_Zarif_meeting_with_UK_foreign_minister_Boris_Johnson_in_Tehran_2017-12-09_02.jpg/330px-Javad_Zarif_meeting_with_UK_foreign_minister_Boris_Johnson_in_Tehran_2017-12-09_02.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1e/Javad_Zarif_meeting_with_UK_foreign_minister_Boris_Johnson_in_Tehran_2017-12-09_02.jpg/440px-Javad_Zarif_meeting_with_UK_foreign_minister_Boris_Johnson_in_Tehran_2017-12-09_02.jpg 2x" data-file-width="800" data-file-height="491" /></a><figcaption>Johnson meeting with Iranian foreign minister <a href="/wiki/Mohammad_Javad_Zarif" title="Mohammad Javad Zarif">Mohammad Javad Zarif</a> in Tehran in December 2017</figcaption></figure>
<p>In a September 2017 op-ed, Johnson reiterated the UK would regain control of £350m a week after Brexit, suggesting it go to the <a href="/wiki/National_Health_Service" title="National Health Service">National Health Service</a> (NHS).<sup id="cite_ref-378" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-378">&#91;374&#93;</a></sup> Cabinet colleagues subsequently criticised him for reviving the assertion and accused of "clear misuse of official statistics" by the chair of the <a href="/wiki/UK_Statistics_Authority" title="UK Statistics Authority">UK Statistics Authority</a>, <a href="/wiki/David_Norgrove" title="David Norgrove">Sir David Norgrove</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-379" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-379">&#91;375&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-beebsplit_380-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-beebsplit-380">&#91;376&#93;</a></sup> The authority rejected the suggestion that it was quibbling over newspaper headlines and not Johnson's actual words.<sup id="cite_ref-beebsplit_380-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-beebsplit-380">&#91;376&#93;</a></sup>
Following the <a href="/wiki/2017_United_Kingdom_general_election" title="2017 United Kingdom general election">2017 general election</a>, Johnson denied media reports he intended to challenge May's leadership.<sup id="cite_ref-381" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-381">&#91;377&#93;</a></sup>
In a February 2018 letter to May, Johnson suggested that Northern Ireland may have to accept border controls after Brexit and that it would not seriously affect trade, having initially said a hard border would be unthinkable.<sup id="cite_ref-382" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-382">&#91;378&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In March 2018, Johnson apologised for his "inadvertent sexism" after being criticised for calling Shadow Foreign Secretary <a href="/wiki/Emily_Thornberry" title="Emily Thornberry">Emily Thornberry</a> as "Lady Nugee"; Thornberry was married to <a href="/wiki/Christopher_Nugee" title="Christopher Nugee">Christopher Nugee</a> but did not use his surname.<sup id="cite_ref-383" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-383">&#91;379&#93;</a></sup> In June, he was reported as having said "fuck business" when asked about corporate concerns regarding a 'hard' Brexit.<sup id="cite_ref-384" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-384">&#91;380&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-385" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-385">&#91;381&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-386" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-386">&#91;382&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-387" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-387">&#91;383&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Johnson said that <a href="/wiki/US_recognition_of_Jerusalem_as_capital_of_Israel" class="mw-redirect" title="US recognition of Jerusalem as capital of Israel">US recognition of Jerusalem as Israel's capital</a> is a "moment of opportunity" for peace.<sup id="cite_ref-388" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-388">&#91;384&#93;</a></sup> In June 2018, Johnson accused the <a href="/wiki/UNHRC" class="mw-redirect" title="UNHRC">UNHRC</a> of focusing disproportionately on the <a href="/wiki/Israeli%E2%80%93Palestinian_conflict" title="Israeli–Palestinian conflict">Israeli–Palestinian conflict</a> and Israel's <a href="/wiki/Israeli-occupied_territories" title="Israeli-occupied territories">occupation</a> of the <a href="/wiki/Palestinian_territories" title="Palestinian territories">Palestinian territories</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-389" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-389">&#91;385&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
